recommender_rubric.justification:
Feasibility (3): The three fallbacks are concrete and conditional, and the tranche-based funding tied to satellite-verified hotspot drops is workable. But the opening package asks for full_to_asean_hms maps and a joint_asean_panel at once. That clashes with Indonesia's stated refusal to release maps and its red line against foreign jurisdiction. The panel's power to request parcel-level data also sits awkwardly with Indonesia's domestic data law. Article 27 says disputes are settled by consultation, with no tribunal, so the panel has no treaty basis and its authority is unclear. The "donors we help direct" funding source is unsupported in the brief.

Tradeoff coverage (3): It covers maps vs sovereignty, attribution vs Indonesian courts, and funding vs verified cuts, and each option states a concession and a risk. It does not address smallholder planting-window impacts in detail. It also omits Singapore's agribusiness lobby and the legal risk of the untested Act. The moratorium is treated only through funding, and the tenure disputes overlapping the concession registry are mentioned only in passing.

Priority consistency (3): Tranche funding against verified cuts and a retained attribution mechanism match Singapore's two red lines. But the headline says to "give up Singapore Act prosecution", which weakens corporate accountability, a core interest. Option 2 concedes active use of the Act and admits it may breach the attribution red line. The rationale also blames the Indonesian authorities, which is not conducive to a deal. The opening package mixes strong asks with concessions.

Counterpart consideration (4): The recommendation explicitly meets Indonesia's red line on foreign jurisdiction, accepts district-level maps, allows partial smallholder exemptions, and offers funding, which addresses Indonesia's fiscal constraint. The attribution-first framing and the blaming rationale limit this. Smallholder protection is only implicit.

Strong arguments (3): It uses the strongest brief points: Section 8 needs maps, Singapore cannot compel enforcement in Indonesia, the Act is untested, and funding should depend on verified results. It leaves out the Act's leverage through civil liability (Section 6) and its listed-company capital-market pressure. It also leaves out Article 8's data-sharing duty as a treaty hook for maps.

Options: 3 options, all distinct. Each addresses a different issue (maps, enforcement, funding).

transcript.position:
Singapore opens with a package built on one idea: the haze cannot be ended unless we can show who owns the land where each fire burns. In 2015 the 24-hour PSI passed 300, schools closed and regional losses ran into the tens of billions of dollars [Background]. Therefore we ask Indonesia to give its full concession maps to the ASEAN Haze Monitoring System, to accept a joint ASEAN panel that reviews attribution and corporate responsibility, and to adopt a peatland moratorium with no exemptions. In return, Singapore will direct donor and development funding through a partial transition fund, released only as measured fire and haze reductions are verified by satellite data. We have not asked for our own Act to be applied to Indonesian companies, because we would rather build a shared mechanism than a contested one.

The most damaging objection is sovereignty: Indonesia says maps are protected by domestic data law and that foreign liability is an intrusion. We answer that the 2002 ASEAN Agreement already makes each party send fire and haze data to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre (Article 8(1)), and that Indonesia kept the right to use its resources only alongside a duty not to damage other states (Article 3(1)) [S1]. Moreover, the Agreement has no court or tribunal, only consultation (Article 27) [S1], so without a joint panel the 2015 dispute has nowhere to be settled. Our own Act is a modest tool: its aggregate fine is capped at S$2 million (section 5(5)) [S2], yet it presumes the owner of burning land caused the haze and lets ownership be proved from maps a foreign government supplies (section 8) [S2]. This shows that maps are the cheap route to accountability, and a joint panel keeps the process regional rather than Singaporean. Singapore will hold back from applying its Act if the maps and panel are in place and work. We cannot accept a settlement with no attribution mechanism, because without one the same dry-season cycle returns and Singaporeans face hazardous air again. We also will not fund transition without measurable reductions, because unconditional money would not stop a single fire.

recommender_rubric.justification:
Scored against the rubric anchors.

Feasibility (3): Option 1 matches Indonesia's round-3 offer of answering panel requests for burned parcels. Option 2 is workable, since both sides accept tranche funding. Option 3 is flagged by the recommendation itself as unlikely, because Indonesia has refused full maps in every round. The "binding" answers within a fixed deadline go beyond what Indonesia offered, and the recommendation doesn't say how they would be enforced.

Tradeoff coverage (3): The options cover maps, enforcement and funding. The moratorium is mentioned only as a side note. Several tensions are covered: tenure disputes, slow verification, funding lagging in an El Nino season, and the agribusiness lobby. The recommendation does not compare the options or rank them, and it doesn't say what Singapore should do if Indonesia rejects all three.

Priority consistency (3): Shelving the Act and tying funding to verified reductions fit Singapore's stated priorities. scores.justification: A joint panel and funding released in tranches against verified hotspot and PSI cuts could be run. judgments.summary: Singapore wants Indonesia to give full concession maps to the regional haze monitoring system so that whoever burns can be identified. In return it would accept a joint ASEAN panel instead of applying its own Act directly. It also asks for a full peatland moratorium with no exemptions and offers a partial donor fund paid in tranches only when haze and hotspot reductions are verified. The case is clear and links each ask to a concession. It is thin on numbers and on the costs it places on Indonesia, and its central ask runs straight into Indonesia's stated objection.
unsupported_claims: Singapore's Act 'already limits its use to proving land ownership': Section 8 allows maps to prove ownership but does not limit how maps are used.
The maps go to a body that parties 'already feed' under Article 8(1): Article 8(1) covers fire and haze data, not concession maps, and the monitoring system is not named in that source.
The claim that funding must be tied to results cites the 2015 moratorium and the Peatland Restoration Agency, which do not contain any verification mechanism.
Full maps are 'the cheapest way' and protect Indonesia from blanket blame: this is an opinion, and no source supports it.

scores.justification: Phased moratorium, Article 8(1) data sharing and district-level aggregated maps are all doable. But full donor funding is not secured and nobody has agreed to pay it. Enforcement by Indonesian courts alone offers no outside check on whether burners are actually pursued.

It names clear package options and conditions, such as district-level maps if funding and enforcement terms are met, and provincial phasing. It gives no amount for the fund, no list of exemptions, no phasing timetable and no data-sharing intervals.

It concedes that 'withholding maps slows attribution of fires'. It does not admit that Indonesian-courts-only leaves Singapore with no remedy for its haze losses. It also does not admit that partial exemptions leave fire-prone peatland open.

This is the opening round. The package matches its stated red lines on foreign jurisdiction and on smallholders. Its offers, such as district-level maps and partial exemptions, are tied to stated conditions.

It engages the specific terms of Singapore's Act: Section 4 reach, the Section 5(5) cap and the Section 8 presumption. It also takes on the 'slows attribution' objection. It does not explain how an attribution mechanism would work without parcel maps.

judgments.summary: Indonesia wants enforcement to stay with its own courts and the concession maps to stay under its control. It offers a phased peatland moratorium with partial exemptions run by provinces, and it will keep sending fire and haze data under the ASEAN agreement. It asks donors and neighbours to fund the transition in full. It argues that Singapore's capped fines are a weak deterrent and that parcel maps would feed foreign liability claims. It is well tied to the legal texts but gives no number for the fund and no route to attribution without maps.
unsupported_claims: The ENSO Diagnostic Discussion of 13 August 2015 and its 'greater than 90%' El Nino probability are not in the scenario or the listed sources.
Unresolved tenure disputes overlap the concession registry, so maps could wrongly name owners: no source supports this.
Applying a foreign Act is 'outside what ASEAN states agreed': Article 3(1) and Article 27 do not say this.
Article 9 means smallholders can only prevent burning if funded: Article 9 imposes a duty on parties and says nothing about funding.
Section 4 would make Indonesia 'accept a foreign court ruling': Section 4 extends the Act's reach, but it does not state how a ruling would bind Indonesia.

unaddressed_tradeoffs: Singapore's government cannot waive private civil suits under Section 6 of its Act, so a joint panel or Indonesian-courts-only deal may not remove liability for companies.
Neither side says how a joint panel would get binding powers when Article 27 provides only for consultation.
Conditional tranche funding pays only after reductions, but smallholders need money up front to give up burning; nobody says how that gap is bridged.
Nobody splits the funding burden among Singapore, other donors and Indonesia, or says what happens if donors do not provide it.
Neither side addresses whether Indonesian courts have the capacity and independence to prosecute powerful concession holders.
Neither side distinguishes smallholders from large corporate concession holders, which matters for both exemptions and liability.
Neither side deals with a possible recurrence of haze during the negotiation or phase-in period.

scores.justification: The package (maps to the monitoring system, joint panel, tranche-based funding checked by the Peatland Restoration Agency) is workable in outline. But it admits the panel needs a mandate that Article 27 does not provide, and it ignores Indonesia's stated red line against foreign jurisdiction. Nobody says who pays for the fund or how large it is.

It gives concrete terms: the S$100,000 daily fine reaches the S$2m cap in 20 days, there is an up-front bridge tranche, later tranches depend on hotspot and PSI reductions, disputed parcels are flagged as unresolved, and exemptions are for smallholders only. It gives no fund size and no definition of 'smallholder'.

It admits that Article 27 gives no binding powers, that Singapore cannot waive private suits under Section 6, and that it is giving up direct application of its Act. It says little about what full parcel maps cost Indonesia in liability exposure.

It opens by listing its moves: a phased moratorium with smallholder exemptions and full donor funding. It holds on full maps and the panel. The new moratorium position is explained as a concession in exchange for maps. One wrinkle is that last round it offered only a partial fund. This is a flagged concession, not an unexplained reversal.

It takes up Indonesia's fines argument and agrees with it, then answers the district-map objection (smallholders and concessions sit side by side) and the tenure-dispute objection (flagging parcels). It does not address Indonesia's red line against foreign jurisdiction beyond saying the Act will not be applied directly.

judgments.summary: Singapore moved to a phased moratorium with smallholder-only exemptions and to full donor funding. It ties both to the release of full parcel maps and an enforcement panel with a written mandate. It proposes safeguards: attribution-only use, flagging disputed parcels, and an up-front smallholder tranche. It says it will not pay if maps are refused. It candidly notes the panel needs a mandate that the treaty does not give.
unsupported_claims: The claim that parcel-level data is required for Section 8 ownership proof is an inference. Section 8 says only that maps supplied by a foreign government can prove ownership, and it does not say what level of detail is needed.
The claim that Article 8(1) 'only requires' fire and haze data to be sent is partly an interpretation of the text.
The claim that Singapore's concession is 'substantial' is not tested against any source.

scores.justification: District maps, Indonesian courts, and verification by the Peatland Restoration Agency are all within Indonesia's own powers. The full moratorium plus full donor funding depends on donors paying an amount that is not costed. Joint costing before the planting window is proposed. Whether Indonesian courts can prosecute powerful concession holders is only asserted.

It offers an up-front smallholder share, tranches tied to verified hotspot reductions, and a joint costing before the planting window. Fund size is explicitly absent. It does not say what the district maps would contain, how often they would be updated, or what 'within days' attribution rests on.

It names the most damaging objections itself: smallholders get no money under tranche-only funding, and Indonesian courts may struggle to prosecute powerful concession holders. It does not admit that district maps leave Singapore with weaker attribution than parcel maps.

It flags its moves: district maps instead of withholding, and a full moratorium instead of partial exemptions. Both are explained as concessions tied to funding. However, it says full donor funding is a condition for the full moratorium, while previously a funded transition was needed for partial exemptions. Accepting a stricter moratorium while keeping its red line against unfunded smallholder restrictions is slightly strained.

It answers Singapore's attribution point directly. It rebuts the panel concession through Article 27 and notes that Section 6 suits remain. It accepts Singapore's wish for a full moratorium and an up-front share. It does not answer Singapore's argument that district maps cannot separate smallholders from large holders.

judgments.summary: Indonesia moved to district-level maps and a full moratorium, and it keeps Indonesian courts only and full donor funding. It argues district maps plus hotspot data are enough to attribute fires. It argues a binding panel has no treaty basis and that Singapore keeps its Section 6 private suits. It accepts an up-front smallholder payment, verification by the Peatland Restoration Agency, and a joint costing of the fund.
unsupported_claims: The claim that district maps plus hotspot data let regional monitors link a fire to an area 'within days' is not backed by any source.
The claim that district data names concession areas, which makes large holders easier to prosecute, is not in the sources and conflicts with the idea that district maps are aggregated.
The ENSO Diagnostic Discussion of 13 August 2015 is cited but is not in the listed sources or the scenario.
The claim that Indonesia has limited fiscal capacity is not supported by the sources.
The claim that Article 9 means smallholders can comply only with funded alternatives is not in Article 9.

unaddressed_tradeoffs: Neither side says who the donors are, how large the fund is, or whether Singapore's donors would actually accept paying a full fund, which affects whether either package is deliverable.

Neither side addresses what happens to large corporate concession holders and to Indonesia's tenure-registry accuracy if the parcel maps are wrong, beyond Singapore's proposal to flag disputed parcels. Neither says who resolves tenure disputes or how long that takes.
Neither side says how verification would work if hotspot reductions are caused by weather (El Nino or rains) and not by the policy, which makes tranche release uncertain.

Neither side deals with the fact that Singapore's Section 6 private suits and Section 8 map presumption could still operate on any maps once they are released to the monitoring system, whatever the attribution-only safeguard says.
Neither side addresses the cost of delay: if there is no agreement before the planting window and the El Nino season, the fire risk goes up for both countries.

scores.justification: A non-binding panel that compares Article 8(1) fire data with district maps and refers named holders to Indonesian courts needs no new treaty power. The fund size and donors are admitted to be unknown, and a joint costing is proposed. The panel's funding, staffing and legal mandate are not described.

It names the panel's functions (compare data, publish districts and concession areas, refer to Indonesian courts), an up-front tranche with later tranches tied to hotspot reductions, rainfall and El Nino notes in PRA reports, and a costing before the planting window. It gives no tranche split, no panel size and no deadline date.

It says 'This costs Singapore the parcel-level maps that Section 8 would use' and accepts that cost. It also admits district maps may not separate large holders from smallholders. It says little about the cost to Indonesia of a publicly named attribution record.

It explains its moves as concessions: district maps instead of parcel maps, and a full moratorium instead of smallholder exemptions. These reverse last round's red line that parcel-level maps are essential and that large concessions stay under a full ban. The attribution red line is redefined to mean a body that compares data and publishes findings. The shift is declared but large, and the full moratorium is a new position.

It takes up Indonesia's Article 27 point and drops binding power. It reuses Indonesia's own claim that district data names concession areas. It answers the smallholder bridge red line and the El Nino concern directly.

judgments.summary: Singapore gives up parcel-level maps and direct application of its Act. It accepts Indonesia's full moratorium and full donor funding. It asks only for a non-binding joint panel that attributes fires from district data and refers named holders to Indonesian courts. Later funding tranches depend on verified hotspot reductions, adjusted for weather. It also proposes a joint costing before the planting window. The proposal is concrete and openly states its costs. Its weakness is that it concedes a lot, reverses its earlier parcel-map red line, and leaves unclear why a non-binding panel does more than Indonesia's own reporting.
unsupported_claims: Its statement that El Nino 'was more than 90% likely' rests on the 13 August 2015 ENSO discussion, which is not among the listed sources, although it is cited in the scenario's argument record.

The claim that Indonesia's PRA can report hotspot counts to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre under Article 8(1) is not supported by that article. It concerns each party's monitoring centre sending data, not the PRA.

scores.justification: Indonesian courts acting on district data, registry checks of flagged fires, and PRA reporting to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre all rely on existing institutions. Prosecution of powerful holders and the tenure disputes it admits are unresolved weaken it. El Nino-adjusted baselines are agreed jointly but not defined.

It specifies registry checks of flagged fires with results reported to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre, phase-in of large concessions first, and an up-front bridge with El Nino-adjusted baselines. It gives no timeline for checks, no fund size and no prosecution commitments, and the 'firm commitment' is not quantified.

It admits unresolved tenure disputes overlap the registry. It names without costing the 'most damaging objection' that a repeat of 2015 goes unanswered. It does not admit that the Singapore side gives up parcel data, enforcement and the panel and gets nothing outside its own courts.

Last round it offered a full moratorium with no exemptions as the trade for full donor funding. It now returns to smallholder exemptions as Singapore proposed, just as Singapore accepts the full moratorium. The change is labelled a concession, but it is a retreat from its own offer and is not explained. The retreat also rests on its own red line about smallholders, which the up-front bridge already met.

It rebuts parcel maps with Singapore's own admission that it cannot waive Section 6 and with Section 8. It does not engage Singapore's new offer: district maps, no application of its Act, a non-binding panel that only refers cases to Indonesian prosecutors. It still argues against a panel 'with enforcement powers', which Singapore dropped.

judgments.summary: Indonesia holds to district maps and Indonesian courts. It proposes registry checks of flagged fires with reports to the regional coordinating centre. It moves to a phased moratorium with smallholder exemptions and asks for full donor funding with an up-front bridge and weather-adjusted baselines. It is firm and uses existing institutions. However, it argues mainly against parcel maps and a binding panel, which Singapore has now dropped. It backtracks on its own full-moratorium offer without a clear reason and does not address the panel Singapore now proposes.
unsupported_claims: That its district maps 'list which concessions lie in each district' and so separate company land from smallholder plots is asserted without support in the scenario or sources.
The claim that unresolved land-tenure disputes overlap the registry has no support in the scenario or sources.
The ENSO Diagnostic Discussion of 13 August 2015 is not a listed source.
The claim that Article 9 means smallholders can stop clearing by fire 'only with funded alternatives' goes beyond what the article says.

unaddressed_tradeoffs: Neither side addresses whether a published attribution record, even a non-binding one, exposes named concession holders to Section 6 private suits in Singapore, which Singapore cannot waive.
Neither side explains who runs, staffs and pays for the panel or the registry checks, or who decides if Indonesia's registry results are accepted when they conflict with the hotspot data.
Neither side explains how disputed tenure entries would be treated in published findings, so innocent holders may be named in a public record.
Neither side addresses the cost to donors and to Singapore of a dry-season delay before the costing and El Nino-adjusted baselines are agreed, while smallholders are restricted or unpaid.
Neither side addresses what happens to the up-front tranche if smallholders still burn, or who recovers it.

recommendation.headline: Give up direct use of our Act and parcel maps to get a panel naming burners

options.condition: Indonesia accepts district maps but rejects any joint panel and offers only its own registry checks
options.action: Accept a non-binding panel that compares hotspot and district data, publishes districts and concession areas, and refers named holders to Indonesian courts. Fund only against verified cuts.
options.requires_concession: Singapore gives up parcel-level maps and any binding enforcement role, and the panel has no treaty power.
options.principal_risk: Panel adds little beyond Indonesia's own reporting, and published findings may expose named holders to Section 6 private suits we cannot waive.

options.condition: Indonesia insists on smallholder exemptions in the moratorium and asks for full donor funding with an up-front bridge
options.action: Accept smallholder-only exemptions if full donor funding is paid in tranches: an up-front bridge, then releases on verified hotspot and PSI cuts, weather-adjusted.
options.requires_concession: Singapore drops its full no-exemptions moratorium and takes a leading role in a joint costing of the fund before the planting window.
options.principal_risk: Exempted peatland stays fire-prone; weather adjustment may let tranches release without real reductions, and no fund size or donors are agreed.

options.condition: Indonesia refuses both a joint panel and any verification of hotspot reductions tied to funding
options.action: Withhold all transition money and keep the Singapore Act available for companies causing haze here, rather than sign a deal with no attribution mechanism.
options.requires_concession: Singapore accepts no deal this dry season, with no funding and no cooperation gains.
options.principal_risk: Delay into the El Nino and planting window risks a repeat of 2015 haze, with PSI above 300 and school closures; the Act's reach is legally untested.

recommendation.rationale: Plantation operators who burn, and the Indonesian authorities who do not stop them, cause the haze; Indonesia and the listed parent companies should carry the enforcement cost, while Singapore pays only against verified reductions. Both sides already agree on district maps and full donor funding, so the live gaps are the panel and the moratorium's exemptions, where we trade the moratorium to hold the panel because it keeps our attribution red line.
recommendation.plain_summary: Offer district-level maps and no direct application of our Act, in exchange for a joint panel that publishes who is burning and funding released only against verified hotspot cuts. Indonesia gets a funded transition; we keep an attribution mechanism and our red lines.

recommender_rubric.justification:
Feasibility (4): The options are conditional on Indonesia's behaviour and rely on mechanisms both sides have already floated. These are a non-binding panel that refers cases to Indonesian courts, tranche funding with an up-front bridge, and a joint costing. The weak spots are that fund size and donors are unspecified, and that the panel has no treaty basis.

Tradeoff coverage (4): The options cover attribution versus sovereignty, exemptions versus fire risk, and funding versus verified reductions. Each carries a stated risk, including Section 6 exposure from published findings, weather adjustment, and El Nino delay. Coverage of the maps issue is thin, because the options treat district maps as settled.

Priority consistency (4): The attribution red line is kept in options 1 and 3. Funding is tied to measurable reductions throughout. The rationale says "we trade the moratorium to hold the panel", but option 2 gives up the full moratorium without linking that to the panel, so the trade is loosely framed. The rationale also blames Indonesian authorities and listed parent companies for bearing the cost, which sits oddly with a settlement built on donor funding, and the "Singapore pays only against verified reductions" line is partly inconsistent with the full-donor-fund opening.

Counterpart consideration (4): The recommendation concedes parcel maps and any binding role, accepts smallholder exemptions, and funds an up-front bridge. These respond directly to Indonesia's red lines. Option 3's threat is less accommodating, though it is a fallback.

Strong arguments (4): It draws on the strongest debate points: the Article 27 non-binding limit, the Section 6 risk, the weather-adjusted baselines, and the up-front bridge. It does not use the S$2 million cap point. The first option's premise that Indonesia would reject any panel is a reasonable anticipation of Indonesia's round 3 position.

Options: 3 options, all distinct. They address different branches of the negotiation: a panel fallback, the moratorium and funding terms, and walk-away.

unsupported_claims: Singapore's own Act already limits use of maps to proving land ownership
debater_rubric.justification: Fully matches Singapore's interests (attribution, corporate accountability) and both red lines. It anticipates Indonesia's sovereignty/data-law objection and answers with Art 8(1). Feasibility gaps: it asks for full maps and a full moratorium while offering only a partial fund. The claim that the Act 'already limits its use to proving land ownership' is not supported by S2. Evidence use is mostly accurate. The fifth claim cites the BRG background for tranche verification, which is only loosely tied.

unsupported_claims: ENSO Diagnostic Discussion of 13 August 2015 gives >90% chance El Nino lasts through 2015-16 northern winter
debater_rubric.justification: Consistent with sovereignty, data-law and smallholder red lines. It correctly uses S2 s5(5), s8, s4 and S1 Art 3(1), 27, 8(1). It anticipates Singapore's attribution objection and offers district maps conditionally. It asks for full donor funding while admitting limited fiscal capacity, which is plausible given its leverage. The El Nino >90% figure comes from an outside ENSO source that is not in the listed sources. The Article 9 citation for smallholders is a stretch.

Directly engages Indonesia's fine-cap point, with correct 20-day arithmetic (S$2m / S$100k). It answers the tenure-dispute worry with a flag-as-unresolved safeguard and links funding to maps. It stays inside its red lines, and the up-front tranche is a sensible bridge. Slight role drift: it concedes full donor funding, though its brief says it funds only against measured reductions, and it admits that this funding is cheap for it. The claim that the exemption is justified because companies do not share livelihoods is only loosely supported by Art 9 and the BRG date. It does not engage the point that a district contains both smallholders and concession holders beyond asserting it.

unsupported_claims: District maps plus hotspot data let regional monitors link a fire to an area within days
debater_rubric.justification: Responds to Singapore's attribution point and to its panel concession, using Art 27 and Section 6 well. It names and answers a real objection about up-front smallholder funds and court capacity. It moves to a full moratorium with no exemptions, which sits oddly with its smallholder red line and the earlier phased approach, and that weakens role consistency. The 'within days' attribution claim is unsupported. It honestly says fund size is not in its sources.

Highly responsive: it accepts Indonesia's Art 27 point, makes the panel non-binding, and refers cases to Indonesian prosecutors. It concedes district maps and a full moratorium. This risks the attribution red line, since district maps cannot separate holders, and it relies on the panel as the mechanism. The weather-adjusted verification via the PRA is a realistic and thoughtful addition. The brief says Singapore lobbies against concession liability, so dropping parcel maps is consistent with that. Evidence use is sound, and it notes that fund size is unknown.

unsupported_claims: District maps list which concessions lie in each district, separating company land from smallholder plots
debater_rubric.justification: It returns to phased exemptions, which fits its smallholder red line. It uses tenure disputes overlapping the registry (in its brief) and Singapore's admission on Section 6 to argue that safeguards cannot bind. It answers the attribution objection with registry checks and PRA reporting, and accepts El Nino-adjusted baselines. It does not engage Singapore's non-binding panel concession, which now only refers cases. The statement that district maps list concessions that already separate company land from smallholders is asserted without a source. The claim that Singapore 'cannot' waive private suits was stated by Singapore in round 2, so it is supported.

transcript.position: Singapore opens by asking for a settlement that can still be used after this haze season ends. Between June and October 2015 the 24-hour PSI passed 300 and schools closed, and regional losses ran into the tens of billions of dollars [Background]. Because the 2002 ASEAN Agreement has no court or tribunal and settles disputes only by consultation (Article 27), it cannot attribute a fire to a company. Therefore we ask Indonesia to give concession maps in full to the ASEAN Haze Monitoring System, so that fires can be tied to the entity that holds the land. We ask for a joint ASEAN panel to review attribution cases, not for Singapore's Act to be applied unilaterally, because we cannot compel enforcement inside Indonesia and extraterritorial prosecution is untested. In return we offer to help fund transition, but only partly and only against measurable reductions in hotspots and PSI days, because we will not pay for a programme that cannot show results. We also ask for a peatland moratorium with no exemptions for existing concessions, since exemptions leave the burning land in the cycle. The strongest objection is sovereignty, and we answer it directly. Article 3(1) keeps Indonesia's right to use its resources, and Article 8(1) already obliges parties to send fire and haze data to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre. Maps going to a regional body under that duty are not a Singapore demand on Indonesian land. Our Act's exposure is also bounded: fines run at S$100,000 a day but are capped at S$2 million in total (s5(2)(a), s5(5)), which is a ceiling of 20 full days, so this is about accountability and not a bid to ruin firms. In return for the maps and panel, Singapore is ready to move on funding size and timing.

key_claims.claim: A regional attribution mechanism is needed because the existing ASEAN treaty cannot assign responsibility for fires, and 2015 showed the cost of that gap.
key_claims.evidence: [S1] Article 27 says disputes are settled by consultation or negotiation with no court or tribunal, while [Background] the 2015 episode pushed PSI above 300 and caused regional losses in the tens of billions of dollars.

key_claims.claim: Giving full concession maps to the ASEAN monitoring system fits Indonesia's existing treaty duties, so it answers the sovereignty objection.
key_claims.evidence: [S1] Article 8(1) requires each party's monitoring centre to send fire and haze data to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre at agreed intervals, and Article 3(1) pairs the sovereign right to use resources with a duty not to damage other states.

key_claims.claim: Maps are the missing link for holding companies accountable, because Singapore's law presumes the landholder caused the haze.
key_claims.evidence: [S2] Section 8 presumes that an entity owning or occupying land where a fire burns caused the haze and allows ownership to be proved from maps supplied by a foreign government.

key_claims.claim: Singapore's penalties are bounded, so Indonesia and its firms face a limited and predictable exposure, not an open-ended one.
key_claims.evidence: [S2] Section 5(2)(a) sets fines up to S$100,000 per day and section 5(5) caps the aggregate at S$2 million, so the cap is reached after 20 days at the maximum daily rate.

concessions: If Indonesia accepts full map sharing with the ASEAN monitoring system and a joint ASEAN panel, Singapore will not insist on applying its own Act to Indonesian conduct.
If maps and the panel are agreed, Singapore can move on the size and schedule of the transition fund, which we will pay in tranches.
red_lines: No settlement without an attribution mechanism: without one, the next dry season repeats 2015, when PSI passed 300 and schools closed, and nobody can be held to account.
No transition funding without measurable reductions: money paid with no hotspot or PSI-day targets cannot be defended to Singapore voters, who go to the polls on 11 September 2015.

transcript.position:
Indonesia shares the goal of ending the haze, but it will do so through its own courts and its own ministries, because the 2002 ASEAN agreement itself rests on sovereignty and consultation. Article 3(1) keeps each party's sovereign right over its resources, and Article 27 settles disputes by consultation with no court or tribunal, so a foreign statute that reaches conduct on Indonesian soil (section 4 of the Singapore Act) goes beyond what ASEAN members agreed to. Therefore enforcement stays with Indonesian courts only. In return, Indonesia will keep sending fire and haze data under Article 8(1), and the Peatland Restoration Agency will report restoration progress to the region. This answers the strongest objection to our proposal, that sovereignty means inaction. It does not, because Indonesia is committing to a moratorium and to restoration, and the real obstacle is money, not will.

Concession maps stay withheld because domestic data law restricts parcel-level disclosure and unresolved tenure disputes overlap the registry. Section 8 of the Singapore Act presumes that whoever owns land where a fire burns caused the haze, and it allows ownership to be proved from maps a foreign government supplies. Releasing parcel maps would therefore feed foreign liability claims, some of them against the wrong owner. On the moratorium, we can accept partial exemptions, with phase-in by provincial administrations through the planting window, but only if donors fully fund the transition. A restriction that falls on smallholders without funded alternatives is a red line, because El Nino conditions have a greater than 90% chance of lasting through the 2015-16 northern winter [Background], so a dry season is coming and a moratorium without alternative livelihoods would push farmers back to burning. Indonesia cannot fund this transition alone. Our offer is conditional: full donor funding and Indonesian-only enforcement in exchange for the moratorium and continued data sharing.

key_claims.claim: A foreign statute reaching conduct on Indonesian soil goes beyond what ASEAN members agreed, so enforcement must stay with Indonesian courts.
key_claims.evidence: [S1] Article 27 settles disputes by consultation or negotiation with no court or tribunal, and Article 3(1) keeps each party's sovereign right over its resources, while [S2] section 4 extends the Singapore Act to conduct outside Singapore.

key_claims.claim: Releasing parcel-level concession maps would let a foreign government build liability cases from them, so maps should be withheld while Indonesia keeps meeting its ASEAN data duty.
key_claims.evidence: [S2] section 8 presumes that an entity owning or occupying land where a fire burns caused the haze and allows ownership to be proved from maps supplied by a foreign government, whereas [S1] Article 8(1) only requires fire and haze data to be sent to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre.

key_claims.claim: The moratorium needs full donor funding, because an unfunded restriction would push smallholders back to fire in a dry year.
key_claims.evidence: El Nino conditions have a greater than 90% chance of lasting through the 2015-16 northern winter [Background], and [S1] Article 9 requires parties to prevent land clearing using fire, which smallholders can only avoid if they have funded alternatives.

key_claims.claim: Singapore's own penalty structure shows that its law is about attributing blame through foreign-supplied evidence, not about preventing fires, which a funded Indonesian programme does.
key_claims.evidence: [S2] section 5(2)(a) sets fines up to S$100,000 per day but section 5(5) caps the total at S$2 million, a small sum next to regional losses in the tens of billions of dollars [Background].

concessions: Indonesia can accept a moratorium with partial exemptions, phased in by provincial administrations, but only if donors fully fund the transition.
Indonesia will keep sending fire and haze data under Article 8(1) and will report Peatland Restoration Agency progress to ASEAN, in return for maps staying withheld.
red_lines: No foreign jurisdiction over acts on Indonesian soil, because it would set a precedent of foreign courts ruling on Indonesian land and let section 8 of the Singapore Act operate against Indonesian owners.
No restriction on smallholders without funded alternatives, because it would push them back to burning during an El Nino dry season.

scores.justification: Sending maps to the ASEAN monitoring system and setting up a joint panel could be done in principle. But the panel has no basis in the 2002 Agreement, which has no tribunal (Art. 27), and it needs Indonesian consent. The tranche funding tied to hotspot and PSI-day targets is workable, but the argument gives no verification method.

The penalty figures are exact (S$100,000 a day, S$2 million cap, 20 days). The package choices are clear. The funding side is vague: no fund size, no tranche schedule, and no hotspot or PSI-day targets, only a promise to 'move on funding size and timing'.

It admits that Singapore cannot compel enforcement in Indonesia, that extraterritorial prosecution is untested, and that it will pay only partly. It does not admit what full maps cost Indonesia or its firms, since s8 would let the maps be used against landholders. It frames the fine cap as reassurance and does not treat the maps as a cost to Indonesia.
This is round 1. The package, the red lines and the concessions (dropping unilateral use of the Act if maps and a panel are agreed) all match the opening statements.
No opponent argument exists yet. It does anticipate the sovereignty objection and answers it with Art. 3(1) and Art. 8(1). It also offers to drop the Act in exchange for the panel.

judgments.summary: Singapore asks Indonesia to give full concession maps to the regional haze monitoring body. It wants a joint ASEAN panel to review who is responsible for fires, instead of applying Singapore's own law. It also wants a peatland moratorium with no exemptions. It offers partial, result-linked funding paid in tranches. It argues that the treaty has no way to assign blame and that its fines are capped. Its weak points are that map-sharing is stretched from the treaty's data duty, the funding is not quantified, and the panel has no legal basis yet.
unsupported_claims: Singapore voters 'go to the polls on 11 September 2015' is not in the scenario or the sources.
Maps going to a regional body fall under the Art. 8(1) duty: Art. 8(1) covers fire and haze data, and the sources do not say it covers concession maps.
'Extraterritorial prosecution is untested' is not supported by the scenario or the sources.

scores.justification: The package depends on donors paying for the whole transition, and none are identified or committed. Singapore has offered only partial funding. Withheld maps combined with Indonesian-only enforcement leaves no route to attribution that Singapore has said it needs.

It makes concrete commitments: continued Art. 8(1) data, Peatland Restoration Agency progress reports to ASEAN, and phase-in by provincial administrations through the planting window. It gives no funding amount, no reporting schedule and no definition of which exemptions.

It admits that 'Indonesia cannot fund this transition alone'. It does not admit that withholding maps and restricting enforcement to Indonesian courts leaves Singapore without any way to hold firms accountable, or that partial exemptions leave burning land in the cycle.

It takes on s8 of the Singapore Act and the fine cap. It addresses the objection that sovereignty means inaction, pointing to the moratorium and restoration. It does not engage Singapore's offer of a joint panel or its offer to drop the Act.

judgments.summary: Indonesia wants enforcement left to its own courts and concession maps withheld. It offers continued fire and haze data and restoration reports. It will accept a moratorium with partial exemptions, but only if donors pay for the whole transition. It says that s8 of Singapore's law could turn the maps into liability cases, and that an unfunded moratorium would push smallholders back to burning in a dry year. Its package is weak on feasibility, because it relies on full outside funding and offers no way to attribute fires. Some of its factual support is not in the sources.

Section 6 of the Singapore Act lets private parties in Singapore sue whatever the two governments agree. Neither side says whether a deal would affect those suits.

recommender_rubric.justification:
Feasibility (4): The three conditional fallbacks (district maps with a review clause, Indonesian courts first with outcome reporting, tranche-based partial fund) sit inside the zone of agreement and are implementable. The opening package is a coherent concession from Singapore's round-1 stance. Weaknesses: the Act-in-reserve clause would likely trip Indonesia's no-foreign-jurisdiction red line, and the tranche mechanism depends on verification that the package itself admits is weak without maps.

Tradeoff coverage (3): Covers the maps, enforcement and funding trade-offs, each with a stated concession and risk. It never addresses the moratorium issue as a trade-off: the package accepts partial_exemptions with no discussion of Singapore's opening demand for full_no_exemptions. It also skips the Section 8 presumption linkage, which is why Indonesia withholds maps, and the Indonesian land-tenure disputes. The headline and rationale say district maps and a joint panel, but option 2 gives up the panel if Indonesia refuses.

Priority consistency (3): The attribution red line is named, and funding is tied to measurable reductions. But district-level maps weaken attribution, which the option itself admits ("only partly met"). The opening package gives away the maps and moratorium positions before any bargaining. The rationale that "plantation companies and Indonesia should bear most restoration cost" leans on an unsupported premise and does not give Singapore a way to hold firms accountable. Indonesia's courts-first fallback has no firm-level attribution mechanism behind it.

Counterpart consideration (4): Directly accommodates Indonesia's sovereignty concern (drop the Act, accept Indonesian courts, aggregated maps), its smallholder red line (exemptions for smallholders), and its fiscal limit (a donor fund). It does not engage the data-law and tenure-dispute constraints in detail, and it offers no answer to Indonesia's demand for full funding beyond tranches.

Strong arguments (3): Uses the untested extraterritorial reach and the inability to enforce inside Indonesia, both strong points from the debate. It does not use the Article 8(1) data-duty argument, the S$2m cap bounded-exposure argument, or the Article 27 no-tribunal gap that justifies a panel. It also ignores Indonesia's strongest point, the El Nino dry-season and smallholder-burning risk, except implicitly through the smallholder exemption.

Options: 3 conditional options, all distinct, because each addresses a different issue (maps, enforcement, funding).

transcript.position:
Singapore asks for a settlement that ends the yearly dry-season cycle, and that needs three things: shared concession maps, an enforcement route that can name the companies responsible, and a moratorium without carve-outs. In 2015 our 24-hour PSI passed 300 and schools closed, so this is a recurring public-health emergency and not a diplomatic irritant. The 2002 ASEAN haze agreement already obliges parties to control open burning (Article 9) and to send fire and haze data to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre (Article 8(1)). However, it has no court or tribunal (Article 27), so without maps nobody can show who owns the burning land. Therefore we propose that Indonesia give full concession maps to the ASEAN Haze Monitoring System, that a joint ASEAN panel review attribution cases, and that the peatland moratorium apply with no exemptions. In return, Singapore will direct a partial donor fund for transition, released in tranches only against measured reductions in hotspots.

The most damaging objection is that sharing maps breaches Indonesian sovereignty and that our Act reaches extraterritorially. We answer that Article 3(1) of the 2002 agreement protects the sovereign right to exploit resources only alongside a duty not to damage other states. Moreover, we are offering a joint ASEAN panel instead of applying our own Act, which means Indonesia keeps a seat in judging its own companies and we do not apply our own law across the border. In return for full maps and a no-exemptions moratorium, we can accept this regional panel route and a donor fund that is partial rather than full. We cannot accept any deal without a working attribution mechanism, because without it the next episode leaves us with no way to identify who burned, and we will not fund transition without measurable reductions, because unconditioned money would leave Singaporeans breathing the same haze.

key_claims.evidence: [S2] section 8 presumes that an entity owning or occupying land where a fire burns caused the haze, and allows ownership to be proved from maps supplied by a foreign government.

key_claims.claim: The existing regional framework cannot settle attribution alone, so a joint ASEAN panel is a necessary addition.
key_claims.evidence: [S1] Article 27 limits dispute settlement to amicable consultation or negotiation, with no court or tribunal, so there is nobody to decide who is responsible.

key_claims.claim: Sharing data is already a treaty duty, so full maps ask Indonesia for nothing beyond the spirit of what it signed.
key_claims.evidence: [S1] Article 8(1) requires each party's monitoring centre to send fire and haze data to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre at agreed intervals, and Article 9 requires parties to prevent land clearing using fire.

key_claims.claim: The harm to Singapore was severe enough to justify firm terms, and our domestic law is calibrated, not punitive.
key_claims.evidence: [Background] PSI passed 300 in 2015 and schools closed; [S2] section 5(2)(a) and 5(5) set fines up to S$100,000 per day with an aggregate cap of S$2 million.

key_claims.claim: Companies, not only states, must answer for burning, and sovereignty is not infringed when a panel and not a foreign court judges them.
key_claims.evidence: [S1] Article 3(1) pairs the sovereign right to exploit resources with a duty not to cause environmental damage to other states.

Singapore will fund only part of transition costs through a donor fund, conditional on a no-exemptions moratorium and disbursement against measured hotspot reductions.

No transition funding without measurable reductions, because unconditioned money would not reduce the PSI exposure Singaporeans face.

transcript.position:
Indonesia wants to stop the haze, and we are ready to act, but the 2002 ASEAN Agreement already says how. Article 3(1) keeps each party's sovereign right over its own resources, and Article 27 sends disputes to consultation, with no court or tribunal. Therefore Indonesian courts, run by Indonesian authorities, must be the only place where acts on Indonesian soil are judged. Singapore's 2014 Act reaches conduct abroad (section 4) and presumes liability from ownership maps supplied by a foreign government (section 8). Handing over parcel-level maps would therefore feed a foreign court case against our own land users. Many of those parcels are also subject to unresolved tenure disputes, so we offer district-level aggregated data instead. This still meets our duty under Article 8(1) to send fire and haze data to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre, and it lets the monitoring system see where fires cluster.

In return for that, Indonesia will implement a moratorium on peatland through provincial administrations, with limited exemptions so that smallholders are not penalised during the planting window. The El Nino outlook gives more than a 90% chance of dry conditions through the 2015-16 northern winter, so we need to act now. A moratorium that falls on smallholders without alternatives would simply push them back to burning, which is why we ask for a full donor fund for the transition. Indonesia cannot pay for this alone, and regional neighbours who suffered the 2015 losses, which ran into tens of billions of dollars, gain far more from a funded transition than from fines they cannot collect on our territory. The most damaging objection is that withholding parcel maps weakens accountability. Our answer is that the maps stay with Indonesian prosecutors, who will enforce under Article 9, and that district-level data lets everyone see results. Our concessions on data and on the moratorium depend on enforcement staying in Indonesian courts and on the transition fund being fully funded.

key_claims.claim: A single Singapore fine regime reaches up to S$100,000 per day of haze and presumes liability from foreign-supplied maps, so sharing parcel-level maps would hand a foreign court the evidence to prosecute our land users.
key_claims.evidence: [S2] section 5(2)(a) sets fines of up to S$100,000 per day, section 5(5) caps the total at S$2 million, and section 8 lets ownership be proved from maps supplied by a foreign government, which is exactly the data we are asked to release.

key_claims.claim: The regional treaty already gives a cooperative path that keeps jurisdiction national, so a foreign or joint tribunal is unnecessary.
key_claims.evidence: [S1] Article 27 settles disputes by consultation or negotiation with no court or tribunal, and Article 3(1) preserves each party's sovereign right over its own resources.

key_claims.claim: District-level aggregated data meets Indonesia's reporting duty while respecting domestic data law and unresolved tenure disputes.
key_claims.evidence: [S1] Article 8(1) requires each party's monitoring centre to send fire and haze data to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre at agreed intervals, and does not require parcel-level concession maps.

key_claims.claim: Urgency is real: a moratorium must start before the dry season peaks, and it only works if smallholders have funded alternatives to burning.
key_claims.evidence: [Background] the 2015 haze pushed Singapore's PSI past 300 and cost tens of billions of dollars, and the ENSO Diagnostic Discussion of 13 August 2015 gives a greater than 90% chance that El Nino lasts through the 2015-16 northern winter.

concessions: Indonesia will give district-level aggregated fire and concession data in place of withholding all maps, but only if enforcement stays with Indonesian courts.
Indonesia will run a peatland moratorium through provincial administrations with partial exemptions, but only if the transition fund is fully funded by donors.
Indonesia will accept regular consultation with ASEAN partners under the 2002 Agreement, without any tribunal.
red_lines: No foreign jurisdiction over acts on Indonesian soil: applying the Singapore Act, or a panel that judges conduct on our land, would put our land users before foreign courts.
No restriction that falls on smallholders without funded alternatives: unfunded limits would push farmers back to burning during the planting window.

transcript.position:
We have moved on two issues: Singapore will now accept smallholder exemptions in the moratorium and a donor fund that covers the full transition cost, in exchange for full concession maps and a joint ASEAN panel that Indonesia can live with. Indonesia's strongest point is that parcel maps would feed a foreign court, because section 8 of our Act lets ownership be proved from maps supplied by a foreign government. We answer that directly: if Indonesia places the maps with the ASEAN Haze Monitoring System, Singapore will commit that they will not be used as evidence under our own Act in Indonesian cases, and the joint panel will only make non-binding attribution findings while Indonesian courts keep the power to prosecute and sentence. That removes the foreign-court risk Indonesia names, and it keeps the one thing we cannot give up, a working way to say who owned the land where a fire burned. Aggregated district data cannot do that, because Article 8(1) of the 2002 agreement covers fire and haze data and does not mention concession maps, so district totals show where fires cluster but not who is responsible.

On the moratorium, Indonesia is right that unfunded limits push smallholders back to burning, so we accept partial exemptions limited to smallholders during the planting window, with none for corporate concessions. In return we accept a full donor fund, which answers Indonesia's demand and the judge's open question about smallholder income, but money is released in tranches only when hotspot counts fall. Hotspots would be measured by the satellite monitoring Singapore already operates and checked by the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre, so verification does not depend on Indonesia's own district data. For the coming dry season, with a greater than 90% chance of El Nino through the northern winter, we propose an interim step: the maps go to the monitoring system first for the highest-risk peat provinces, and the first fund tranche pays for smallholder alternatives there. If Indonesia accepts full maps and the panel for attribution, we will not insist on a no-exemptions moratorium. If it refuses any attribution route, we cannot sign, and no fund tranche is released without measured reductions.

key_claims.evidence: [S2] section 5(5) caps aggregate fines at S$2 million, against regional losses in the tens of billions of dollars and a 24-hour PSI above 300 in 2015 [Background].

key_claims.claim: Urgency favours an interim arrangement now, with smallholder exemptions funded and fund payments tied to measured hotspot reductions.
key_claims.evidence: [Background] the ENSO Diagnostic Discussion of 13 August 2015 gives a greater than 90% chance that El Nino persists through the 2015-16 northern winter, and Singapore's PSI passed 300 in 2015.

transcript.position:
We have moved on the moratorium: Indonesia now accepts a peatland moratorium with no exemptions, which is Singapore's top ask on that issue, but only if the transition fund is fully funded and enforcement stays in Indonesian courts. Singapore's strongest point is that without maps nobody can show who owns burning land, and that Article 27 has no tribunal. We answer that attribution does not need a foreign panel or parcel maps shared abroad. Indonesian prosecutors hold the parcel data and will act on it, while district-level data sent to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre under Article 8(1) lets partners see where fires cluster. Section 8 of Singapore's Act presumes liability from foreign-supplied maps, so releasing them would hand a foreign court evidence against our land users. A joint panel judging fires on our soil would also be foreign jurisdiction by another name, which we cannot accept.

In return for giving up exemptions, we ask Singapore to see that a ban with no exemptions falls on smallholders, so a partial fund would push them back to burning during the planting window. That is why the fund must be full, and we accept Singapore's condition that money be released in tranches against measured hotspot reductions. To answer the unresolved measurement question, hotspot counts would be taken from satellite data by the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre, which needs no parcel maps, and reported by district. For the coming El Nino dry season, we will have provincial administrations start the moratorium and publish prosecutions under Article 9 before maps or funds are finalised. Our most vulnerable point is accountability without joint adjudication, so Indonesia will report case outcomes to ASEAN partners through the consultation process in Article 27. If Singapore accepts Indonesian courts and a full fund, we can talk about wider data sharing later.

scores.justification: A tranche-based partial donor fund tied to hotspot reductions and a joint ASEAN panel are workable in principle. But the panel has no legal basis in the treaty (Article 27 gives none), and full maps are something Indonesia has refused. The text does not say who sits on the panel or who pays the donor fund.

It names four package items and a conditional release of funds 'in tranches only against measured reductions in hotspots'. It gives no tranche sizes, no hotspot targets, no panel composition or procedure, and no fund size.

It admits that dropping direct application of its own Act is a concession, and that Indonesia has sovereignty objections. It does not admit that the no-exemption moratorium burdens smallholders, or that full maps expose Indonesian land users to liability.
The package, the concessions and the red lines match the opening statements. The panel and partial fund appear as the same conditional offers throughout.

It takes on the sovereignty objection directly with Article 3(1) and offers a panel instead of the Singapore Act. It does not answer Indonesia's point about tenure disputes or about smallholders needing alternatives.

judgments.summary: Singapore asks for full concession maps shared with the ASEAN monitoring system, a joint ASEAN panel to review who is responsible, a moratorium with no exemptions, and a partial donor fund released only as hotspots fall. It offers to forgo its own Act in Indonesian cases and to fund only part of the cost. The case is clear and consistent. It is thin on numbers and on the cost to smallholders. It also stretches Article 8(1) to cover concession maps.

The claim that sovereignty is not infringed when a panel judges companies is not supported by Article 3(1), which says nothing about panels.
The statement that Singapore's Act is 'calibrated, not punitive' rests on the fine figures only, and these do not show that.
'Singapore will direct a partial donor fund' implies a donor source that nothing in the scenario supports.

scores.justification: District-level data and a moratorium run through provincial administrations can be done. The whole package depends on a full donor fund with no funder identified, and on Indonesian courts alone, which Singapore rejects.
It cites S$100,000 per day, the 90% El Nino probability and a district data scale. It gives no exemption terms, no planting-window dates, no fund size and no prosecution targets.

It engages directly with how section 8 and section 5 would turn shared maps into evidence in a foreign court. It does not respond to Singapore's argument that Article 27 leaves nobody to decide attribution.

judgments.summary: Indonesia offers district-level aggregated fire and concession data, a moratorium with limited exemptions run by provinces, enforcement only in Indonesian courts, and a fully funded donor transition. scores.justification: Offers a workable design: maps held by the monitoring system, non-binding panel findings, tranches tied to satellite hotspot counts checked by the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre, and an interim step for the highest-risk peat provinces. Weaknesses: it never says who pays the full fund or how large it is, and it assumes Indonesia will place full maps with a regional body, which Indonesia has refused.

Gives concrete mechanics: smallholder-only exemptions in the planting window, none for corporate concessions, a first tranche for smallholder alternatives in high-risk provinces, later tranches only on verified hotspot falls, and a pledge not to use the maps under its own Act in Indonesian cases. It gives no fund size, tranche schedule or hotspot-reduction threshold.

It admits it is giving up the no-exemptions moratorium, a partial fund and use of its own Act, and it names the foreign-court risk Indonesia fears. It says little about what full maps cost Indonesia beyond that risk, such as the tenure disputes and domestic data law. It also plays down the panel's reputational and sovereignty cost, and it calls fine exposure 'modest', which dismisses Indonesia's worry about the precedent.

Moves from a no-exemptions moratorium to smallholder exemptions and from a partial to a full fund, and says so explicitly as concessions. Full maps, a panel and the attribution red line are kept. The panel is now non-binding, which is explained as a response to Indonesia's objection.

Takes up Indonesia's strongest point, that section 8 maps would feed a foreign court, and answers it with a commitment not to use them as evidence. It also accepts Indonesia's smallholder argument and its demand for a full fund. Its answer on the planned verification of hotspots, using satellite data, meets Indonesia's earlier concern about data.

judgments.summary: Singapore moved toward Indonesia on three points: smallholder exemptions, a full donor fund, and a pledge not to use the maps under its own Act. It kept two firm demands: full maps held by the regional monitoring system, and a panel that can name owners of burning land, with non-binding findings. Fund payments stay tied to satellite-verified hotspot reductions, and it proposes an interim step for the highest-risk peat provinces this dry season. The weak points are an undefined fund size and funder, and that it assumes Indonesia will accept regional custody of the maps.
unsupported_claims: Singapore already operates satellite monitoring of hotspots that could be used for verification (not in the scenario or sources).
Reference to 'the judge's open question about smallholder income' is not in the scenario or sources.

recommender_rubric.justification: Feasibility (3): The options are conditional fallbacks tied to specific Indonesian refusals, and the tranche mechanism is workable. But option 1 asks Indonesia for parcel maps on flagged fires, which Indonesia has refused in both rounds. Option 2 relies on a panel trigger after Indonesian courts decline to act, and that trigger runs into Indonesia's red line against foreign jurisdiction. Tradeoff coverage (3): The options cover maps, enforcement and funding. The moratorium appears only in the rationale and the opening package, with no fallback option. The recommendation never says who the other donors are, and it only partly addresses the El Nino timing. It does flag risks such as hotspots rising from weather and the legally untested extraterritorial reach. Priority consistency (3): The attribution red line is kept, and funding is tied to measured reductions. But the opening package of full maps, a joint panel and a full donor fund is incompatible with the stated headline of dropping our own Act. It also contradicts the rationale's claim that Singapore will pay only against verified results, because it pays a first tranche up front. The rationale also says the fund pays for smallholders but names no non-Singapore funder. Counterpart consideration (4): It takes up Indonesia's sovereignty concern by pledging not to use maps under our Act, accepting Indonesian prosecution first, and bridging smallholders. It does not engage with Indonesia's refusal of any panel, or with tenure disputes and domestic data law. Strong arguments (3): It uses the strongest debate moves, namely the non-use pledge, satellite-verified tranches and the moratorium with no exemptions. It does not use the strongest Singapore point that Article 8(1) does not cover concession maps. The rationale's blame framing, that Indonesian authorities cause the haze, is not supported by the sources and is unlikely to help the negotiation. transcript.position:
Singapore opens with a package built around attribution, because without it the 2015 episode repeats every dry season. Our 24-hour PSI passed 300, schools closed, and regional losses ran into the tens of billions of dollars [Background], yet the ASEAN Agreement has no court or tribunal and settles disputes only by consultation [S1 Article 27]. Therefore we ask that Indonesia's concession maps go to the ASEAN Haze Monitoring System, which Article 8(1) already fits because monitoring centres must send fire and haze data to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre. We also ask for a joint ASEAN panel to decide who is responsible, and a full peatland moratorium without exemptions, since peatland fires are the source of the haze.

The most damaging objection is that this violates Indonesian sovereignty. We answer that our Act is modest: its aggregate fine is capped at S$2 million [S2 section 5(5)], and Article 3(1) of the ASEAN Agreement already pairs sovereign use of resources with a duty not to damage other states. A joint panel, rather than applying our Act inside Indonesia, keeps judgment in a regional body and so respects sovereignty more than our own statute would. In return, Singapore will direct a partial donor fund for peatland transition, but only if it is tied to measurable reductions in fire and haze, because we will not pay for transition without results and we will not sign a settlement with no attribution mechanism. If Indonesia accepts the map-sharing and the panel, we can discuss the size of the fund and phasing of the moratorium. We also note that Singapore's Parliament was dissolved on 25 August 2015 and polling is on 11 September [Background], so we cannot appear to trade away accountability for the haze.

key_claims.claim: Without an attribution mechanism, the recurring haze cannot be tied to specific companies, because the ASEAN Agreement has no court or tribunal.
key_claims.evidence: [S1] Article 27: disputes are settled amicably by consultation or negotiation and there is no court or tribunal, so only a new joint panel can fill the gap.

key_claims.claim: Concession maps are the cheapest route to attribution, because ownership of burning land can be proved from them.
key_claims.evidence: [S2] section 8: an entity owning or occupying land where a fire burns is presumed to have caused the haze, and ownership can be proved from maps supplied by a foreign government.

key_claims.claim: Sharing fire and haze data with ASEAN is already an Indonesian treaty duty, so map-sharing is not a new sovereignty burden.
key_claims.evidence: [S1] Article 8(1): each party's monitoring centre must send fire and haze data to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre at agreed intervals.

key_claims.claim: Singapore's own law is restrained, which answers the extraterritoriality objection.
key_claims.evidence: [S2] section 5(5): the aggregate fine is capped at S$2 million, against regional losses in the tens of billions of dollars [Background].

key_claims.claim: The cost of inaction is very large, which justifies a firm moratorium and monitored funding.
key_claims.evidence: [Background] PSI passed 300 in the hazardous band in 2015, schools closed, and regional losses ran into the tens of billions of dollars.

concessions: We will drop our demand to apply the Singapore Act directly in Indonesia and accept a joint ASEAN panel, if Indonesia shares full concession maps with the ASEAN Haze Monitoring System.
We will fund a partial donor transition fund, if payments are tied to measurable reductions in fire and haze.

transcript.position: Indonesia accepts that the 2015 haze, when Singapore's 24-hour PSI passed 300 between June and October [Background], must not recur, and we are ready to act on our own soil through the Peatland Restoration Agency, created in January 2016 [Background]. However, enforcement on Indonesian territory belongs to Indonesian courts. The 2002 ASEAN Agreement, which both sides signed, keeps each party's sovereign right to use its resources and settles disputes by consultation, with no court or tribunal at all [S1 Articles 3(1) and 27]. Singapore's Act reaches conduct outside Singapore and presumes liability from maps supplied by a foreign government [S2 sections 4 and 8]. Handing over concession maps would therefore feed a foreign court's presumption against firms and smallholders on our land, and our data law bars parcel-level disclosure. Our treaty duty is to send fire and haze data from our monitoring centre to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre [S1 Article 8(1)], and we will keep doing that. We therefore propose that Indonesian courts alone enforce, that concession maps stay withheld, and that the moratorium carry partial exemptions so that smallholders are not pushed off their land during the planting window.\n\nThe strongest objection to this is that Indonesia is shielding offenders while El Nino conditions, with a greater than 90% chance of lasting through the 2015-16 northern winter [Background], raise the fire risk. Our answer is that a moratorium only works if farmers can comply, so a restriction on smallholders must come with money. We therefore ask for a fully funded donor transition fund, paid by those who gain most from clean air, and in return Indonesia will accept a moratorium that covers new clearing of peatland with limited exemptions for existing smallholder plots. If Singapore accepts Indonesian courts and the funded moratorium, we can discuss sharing district-level aggregated fire-risk information, because that lets Singapore's monitors see where the risk lies without exposing parcel-level data. Without funding and without Indonesian jurisdiction, we cannot move.

key_claims.claim: Indonesian courts alone should enforce, because the regional treaty provides no court and no foreign tribunal for acts on Indonesian soil.
key_claims.evidence: [S1] Article 27 says disputes are settled amicably by consultation or negotiation with no court or tribunal, so applying Singapore's Act would go beyond what both parties agreed in 2002.

key_claims.claim: Concession maps should stay withheld because Singapore's Act would turn them into evidence of presumed liability.
key_claims.evidence: [S2] section 8 presumes that the owner or occupier of land where a fire burns caused the haze and allows ownership to be proved from maps supplied by a foreign government, so supplying maps would hand a foreign court the proof it needs.

key_claims.claim: Indonesia already meets its treaty data duty and does not need to give maps to meet it.
key_claims.evidence: [S1] Article 8(1) requires each party's monitoring centre to send fire and haze data to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre at agreed intervals, which covers fire and haze data and does not mention plantation concession maps.

key_claims.claim: Singapore's penalties show the Act is about liability claims against firms, not about stopping fires, so funding prevention at home is the better use of money.
key_claims.evidence: [S2] section 5(2)(a) sets fines up to S$100,000 per day, capped at S$2 million in total under section 5(5), and section 6 lets private parties sue, whereas a donor fund pays for alternatives to burning for smallholders.

transcript.position: We have moved on three issues since last round: we now accept partial exemptions limited to smallholders and a fully funded donor transition, and in return we hold firm on full concession maps and a joint panel. Indonesia's strongest point is that maps would feed a foreign court's presumption of liability against firms and smallholders [S2 section 8]. Our answer is that under our proposal the maps go to the ASEAN Haze Monitoring System, not to a Singapore court, and a joint ASEAN panel, not our Act, would weigh them. Plots with disputed tenure would be flagged so that no smallholder is presumed liable on a contested boundary. Article 8(1) already obliges Indonesia's monitoring centre to send fire and haze data to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre [S1], so map-sharing is a narrow extension of that channel. It is not a transfer of jurisdiction, and we withdraw our demand to apply our Act inside Indonesia, which Indonesia's red line rejected.\n\nIndonesia has told us it cares most about who enforces and who pays. We can meet the second: if Indonesia accepts full maps and the joint panel, we will back a fully funded donor transition, paid in tranches only after the verified fire and haze reductions that our red line requires. Verification would use satellite hotspot data through the ASEAN monitoring system, so the fund is not paid on promises. We also accept partial exemptions in the moratorium, but only for smallholder plots, while large plantation companies, which can afford alternatives to burning, get no exemption. This answers the funding lag before the next dry season: the first tranche would pay smallholders for fire-free clearing during the El Nino window, which has a greater than 90% chance of lasting through the 2015-16 northern winter [Background]. The panel would also not extinguish the private right to sue under section 6 of our Act [S2], since Singapore residents who suffer losses keep that right. We would, however, consider deferring suits against any firm that the panel is actively handling and that complies with its findings. Without attribution, Article 27 leaves only consultation and no tribunal [S1], and the haze that closed schools in 2015 would return.

transcript.position: We have moved since round one: Indonesia now offers district-level concession information and a full moratorium without exemptions, and in return holds firm on Indonesian courts and a fully funded transition. Singapore's strongest point is that without attribution the 2015 episode repeats, because the ASEAN Agreement has no court or tribunal [S1 Article 27]. We accept the problem and answer it without a foreign forum. Indonesia will give the ASEAN Haze Monitoring System concession information aggregated by district, which shows which districts and which concession blocks are burning, and Indonesian courts will act on the fire and haze data that our monitoring centre already sends under Article 8(1) [S1]. Full parcel-level maps are not needed for this. Singapore's own section 8 presumes liability from ownership maps [S2 section 8], and with unresolved land-tenure disputes overlapping the registry, a parcel map would risk presuming guilt against smallholders on disputed land. A joint panel is also not neutral for us, because it would still rule on acts on Indonesian soil, and that is a red line.\n\nThe most damaging objection to our offer is that Indonesian courts alone are a promise with no verification. We answer by offering a verification route that does not touch our jurisdiction: the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre receives our fire and haze data [S1 Article 8(1)], and donor payments can be released against its reported reductions in fire hotspots. The time lag matters too: with El Nino conditions likely to last through the 2015-16 northern winter [Background], we ask that the first donor tranche be paid before the next dry season, otherwise the moratorium lands on smallholders unfunded and we cannot sign.

transcript.position: We have moved on the moratorium: Indonesia now accepts partial exemptions limited to smallholders, which is the very position Singapore offered last round, and we also offer a company-level reporting step on top of district data, but we hold firm on Indonesian courts and a fully funded transition.
