Singapore has also dropped direct application of its Act, so the remaining gap between us is small: who rules. Our answer is that Indonesian courts rule, and in return we give Singapore something it needs. Where district data shows a burning concession block, the Indonesian government will tell the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre which licensed company holds that block, and will report publicly on what the courts did. That meets the judge's question about how district data reaches a specific company, because the block-level licence holder is named while parcel maps stay in Indonesia. Parcel maps would be dangerous here because section 8 presumes the owner or occupier of burning land caused the haze, and maps can be supplied by a foreign government [S2 section 8]. With unresolved tenure disputes overlapping our registry, that presumption could fall on smallholders on contested plots.\n\nThe most damaging objection to this offer is that payment against verified reductions cannot arrive before the next dry season, so smallholders carry the cost with no money in hand, and that El Nino could push fire counts up despite compliance. We answer with a design. The first tranche is paid in advance to smallholders for fire-free clearing, because El Nino has a greater than 90% chance of lasting through the 2015-16 northern winter [Background]. Later tranches are released against reductions reported through the ASEAN channel [S1 Article 8(1)], but measured against compliance on funded plots and adjusted for El Nino, so a dry year does not cancel payment for farmers who stopped burning. Because Singapore weights funding less than we do, we ask it to back a fully funded donor transition, and in return we accept partial exemptions and company-level disclosure. Smallholders on disputed land would be covered by funded alternatives and not cut off, because our red line bars any restriction on them without funded alternatives.

A full moratorium with no exemptions is hard to carry out for smallholders, and the argument does not say how it would work.

In return it offers to drop direct use of its own Act in Indonesia and to pay into a partial donor fund, but only if the money is tied to measured fire and haze cuts. The case is clear and gives up something real. It is thin on how the panel would be set up and how large the fund would be. This is the opening round. The package follows from its stated red lines (no foreign jurisdiction, no unfunded smallholder restrictions). The aggregated-data offer is explicitly conditional and deferred.

It adds a new offer to name the licence holder of each burning block to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre and to publish court outcomes. It also proposes an advance first tranche and El Nino-adjusted later payments. The sides already agree on district maps and a full donor fund, so the real gaps are who rules (panel or Indonesian courts) and moratorium exemptions.
recommendation.plain_summary: Offer district-level maps, a fully funded transition paid in tranches against verified fire reductions, and no direct use of our Act in Indonesia. In return ask for a joint ASEAN panel that verifies company-level findings and a full moratorium, so we keep an attribution route and pay only for results.

recommender_rubric.justification:
Feasibility (4): The options track the live Round 3 gap. Option 1 is a panel that verifies and publishes findings, with sanctions left to Indonesian courts and Indonesia naming licence holders. Option 3 is a ring-fenced advance tranche, with later tranches released against dryness-adjusted hotspot reductions. Both match terms the two sides have already put on the table. A gap remains: option 1 still needs a panel that "verifies" without "ruling". Indonesia's red line rejects any panel ruling on its conduct, and the recommendation doesn't say how to square that.

Tradeoff coverage (3): It covers attribution against sovereignty, the advance tranche against the risk of losing money, and exemptions against uncontrolled burning. It does not address the Singapore agribusiness lobby or listed plantation parents. It does not cover Indonesia's data law or the fund's size and donor shares. It also says little about how Singapore would use the section 6 suit deferral as leverage, or about the fiscal split. The rationale's "real gaps" are the panel and exemptions, which is correct, but the options skip the maps and funding questions.

Priority consistency (4): Both red lines are protected. Option 2 walks away rather than accept no attribution mechanism, and payment is tied to measured reductions. The headline says "Give up parcel maps and direct use of our Act", which is consistent with the concessions Singapore has already made. The opening package keeps the full moratorium with no exemptions, yet option 3 accepts smallholder exemptions. That is a mild inconsistency, though it is a negotiating sequence and not a clash of priorities. The rationale also says Singapore "should pay only against measured reductions", but option 3 pays an advance tranche. That is justified as a ring-fenced exception, and the recommendation flags it as a risk.

Counterpart consideration (4): It engages Indonesia's sovereignty concern. It leaves sanctions to Indonesian courts, drops the Act, flags disputed-tenure plots and accepts smallholder exemptions. It also answers the planting-window and funding-lag concerns with the advance tranche. It is weaker on Indonesia's red line against any panel ruling. Option 2 pushes the panel hard as a condition, and the rationale blames Indonesian "licensing authorities", which is adversarial toward the counterpart.

Strong arguments (4): It uses the strongest debate points. These are the verify-and-refer panel, naming licence holders, an advance tranche, dryness adjustment and the Article 27 gap in the treaty. Citations to specific sources are thin in the recommendation itself. It also leaves out the section 8 presumption and disputed-tenure arguments except for the brief mention of flagging.

Options: 3 options, all distinct. They cover the enforcement compromise, the walk-away condition and the funding and exemptions trade.

transcript.position: Singapore asks for a settlement that ends the recurring dry-season haze and can still be used after this episode is forgotten. Between June and October 2015 our 24-hour PSI passed 300, schools closed and regional losses reached the tens of billions of dollars [Background], so the status quo is costing every party in the region far more than any single measure on the table. The core of our proposal is that Indonesia's agencies share full plantation concession maps with the ASEAN Haze Monitoring System. Without maps nobody can say whose land is burning, and Article 8(1) of the ASEAN Agreement already obliges each party's monitoring centre to send fire and haze data onward, so this extends an existing duty rather than creating a new one. In return for those maps, Singapore will not insist that its own Act be applied inside this settlement. We propose instead a joint ASEAN panel to review attribution cases, because the 2002 Agreement has no court or tribunal at all (Article 27) and consultation alone has not stopped the fires.\n\nWe expect Indonesia to object that sharing maps offends sovereignty. However, Article 3(1) of the Agreement protects the right to exploit resources only alongside a duty not to damage other states, and a panel run by ASEAN gives Indonesia a seat that Singapore's own courts would not. We also expect the objection that our Act is overreaching. It is modest: fines run at up to S$100,000 per day and are capped at S$2 million in total [S2], so it is a deterrent signal, not a threat to Indonesian revenue, and we are willing to hold it back if the panel and maps are in place. We ask for a full peatland moratorium with no exemptions, since existing concessions are where the fires burn, and we will back a partial donor fund for transition, paid in tranches only when satellite data show measured reductions in hotspots. We will not sign a deal without an attribution mechanism, and we will not fund transition without measurable reductions, because unconditional money would repeat the 2015 outcome at our taxpayers' expense.

key_claims.claim: Haze in 2015 reached hazardous levels in Singapore and imposed regional losses in the tens of billions of dollars, so the cost of continued inaction exceeds the cost of sharing data and funding transition.
key_claims.evidence: [Background] Between June and October 2015 Singapore's 24-hour PSI passed 300, schools closed, and regional economic losses ran into the tens of billions of dollars.

key_claims.claim: Sharing concession maps with the ASEAN monitoring system extends a duty Indonesia already accepted, so it does not create a new sovereignty burden.
key_claims.evidence: [S1] Article 8(1) requires each party's monitoring centre to send fire and haze data to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre at agreed intervals, and maps are what turn that data into attribution.

key_claims.claim: A joint ASEAN panel fills a gap in the 2002 Agreement, which has no binding dispute forum, and is a concession from Singapore's own Act.
key_claims.evidence: [S1] Article 27 says disputes are settled by consultation or negotiation with no court or tribunal, and [S2] section 4 shows Singapore could otherwise apply its Act to conduct outside Singapore.

key_claims.claim: Singapore's Act is a limited deterrent, not a threat to Indonesian revenue, which answers the overreach objection.
key_claims.evidence: [S2] section 5(2)(a) sets fines of up to S$100,000 per day and section 5(5) caps the aggregate at S$2 million; section 8 presumes the land occupier caused the fire, provable from maps supplied by a foreign government.

concessions: Singapore will not insist on applying its own Act inside this settlement, if full concession maps go to the ASEAN monitoring system and a joint ASEAN panel hears attribution cases.
Singapore will back a partial, not full, donor fund for transition, if tranches are released only against measured hotspot reductions.
red_lines: No settlement without a working attribution mechanism, because without it the next dry-season fires cannot be traced to any landholder and the 2015 cycle repeats.
No transition funding without measurable reductions, because unconditioned money gives donors and Singapore taxpayers no protection against another PSI above 300.

transcript.position: Indonesia accepts that the 2015 haze, with Singapore's 24-hour PSI above 300 and regional losses in the tens of billions of dollars, must not be repeated, and with a greater than 90% chance that El Nino lasts through the 2015-16 northern winter, the next fire season is a real danger. However, the fastest way to stop fires is to fund and enforce action on the ground, not to import foreign liability law. Therefore we propose that Indonesian courts and the Indonesian government remain the only enforcers on Indonesian soil. The 2002 ASEAN Agreement already gives parties the sovereign right to use their resources (Article 3(1)) and settles disputes by consultation, with no tribunal (Article 27). Singapore's Act reaches conduct abroad (section 4), lets private suits proceed whether or not the conduct is actionable where it happened (section 6), and presumes the landowner caused the haze using maps supplied by a foreign government (section 8). That would put Indonesian acts before a foreign forum, which we cannot accept.\n\nIn return for that, Indonesia offers real transparency and a real moratorium. We can give the ASEAN monitoring system concession data aggregated by district, which fits the data-sharing duty in Article 8(1) while respecting our domestic data law and the unresolved tenure disputes that overlap the registry. Parcel-level maps would turn disputed boundaries into court evidence in Singapore, so we hold them back. We can also have provincial administrations and the Peatland Restoration Agency apply a moratorium with limited exemptions, which is a concession on an issue where we have room to move. This moves only if a donor fund covers the transition in full, because a ban that falls on smallholders with no alternative income would fail in the field and push people back to burning during the planting window. The most damaging objection is that district-level data is too coarse to catch culprits. Our answer is that district data lets the monitoring system target the fire hotspots, and that Indonesian enforcement, backed by funded alternatives, is what actually removes the incentive to burn. If donors accept the funding and the enforcement principle, we can discuss the speed of data sharing.

key_claims.claim: Singapore's Act would expose acts on Indonesian soil to a foreign legal process, with exposure far beyond the headline fine cap of S$2 million.
key_claims.evidence: [S2] section 5(5) caps the criminal fine at S$2 million, but section 6 lets anyone in Singapore sue for injury, property damage or economic loss without a cap and whether or not the conduct is actionable abroad, so the real exposure is open-ended, and the 2015 losses ran in the tens of billions of dollars [Background].

key_claims.claim: The ASEAN regional framework already settles disputes by consultation and leaves enforcement with the territorial state, so Indonesian-only enforcement is consistent with it.
key_claims.evidence: [S1] Article 27 says disputes are settled amicably by consultation or negotiation with no court or tribunal, and Article 3(1) preserves each party's sovereign right to exploit its own resources, so foreign judicial enforcement has no basis in the agreement.

key_claims.claim: District-level concession data meets the agreed data-sharing duty without exposing disputed parcels to foreign courts.
key_claims.evidence: [S1] Article 8(1) requires fire and haze data to be sent to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre at agreed intervals, and [S2] section 8 lets Singapore prove land ownership from foreign-government maps, so parcel-level maps would become evidence in presumption-of-liability cases while tenure disputes remain unresolved.

key_claims.claim: A moratorium can work only if smallholders have a funded alternative, because the fire danger is imminent.
key_claims.evidence: A greater than 90% chance of El Nino lasting through the 2015-16 northern winter (ENSO Diagnostic Discussion, 13 August 2015) means the dry-season fire risk is immediate, and Indonesia created the Peatland Restoration Agency in January 2016 [Background] to restore peatland, which needs donor money because our fiscal capacity cannot carry it alone.

concessions: Conditional on full donor funding and Indonesian-only enforcement, Indonesia will share concession data aggregated by district with the ASEAN monitoring system.
Conditional on full transition funding, Indonesia will apply a moratorium with limited exemptions rather than a blanket exemption for existing concessions.
red_lines: No foreign jurisdiction over acts on Indonesian soil: Singapore's Act cannot be applied to conduct in Indonesia, because section 6 civil suits and section 8 presumptions would put Indonesian landholders before a foreign court.
No restriction that falls on smallholders without funded alternatives: a ban without income support would hit farmers during the planting window and push them back to burning.

transcript.position: We have moved on two issues since last round: Singapore now accepts limited exemptions in the moratorium and will back a full donor fund, provided every tranche is tied to verified fire reductions, and in return we hold firm on full concession maps and a joint ASEAN panel. Indonesia's strongest point is that Singapore's Act would put acts on Indonesian soil before a foreign forum, and that civil suits under section 6 carry no cap even though the criminal fine is capped at S$2 million [S2]. We answer that directly: a joint ASEAN panel is the forum for attribution in this settlement, and Singapore will state that it will not bring section 6-style claims or rely on the section 8 presumption against Indonesian landholders for conduct covered by the panel's process, so long as the maps are shared and the panel works. That removes the open-ended exposure Indonesia fears and keeps enforcement from sitting in a foreign court. Indonesian courts alone are not enough, because the 2002 Agreement has no tribunal (Article 27) and consultation alone did not prevent a PSI above 300 in 2015 [S1][Background].\n\nWhat Indonesia seems to care about most is a funded transition for smallholders and keeping parcel disputes out of foreign courts. We meet the first by moving from a partial fund to a full donor fund, which costs us little because transition funding matters least to us, but we require that money be released in tranches against hotspot reductions measured by satellite and checked by the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre, with a weather adjustment so that a drought year does not automatically cut funding or reward failure. We meet the second by restricting map access to the monitoring system and the panel, which fits Article 8(1), rather than publishing parcels. The most damaging objection to us is that full maps expose disputed tenure. Our answer is that district-level data cannot show whose land is burning, so it cannot support any attribution, and Singapore will not sign a deal without an attribution mechanism. The panel can also set aside parcels under a recorded tenure dispute until they are resolved. If Indonesia accepts full maps and the panel, we accept limited exemptions for existing concessions and the full fund.

key_claims.claim: District-level data cannot attribute fires to a landholder, so full maps restricted to the monitoring system and the panel are the minimum for a working attribution mechanism.
key_claims.evidence: [S1] Article 8(1) already requires fire and haze data to be sent to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre at agreed intervals, and [S2] section 8 shows that ownership is proved from maps, so aggregated district figures would leave the 2015 episode, with PSI above 300 [Background], unattributable.

key_claims.claim: A joint ASEAN panel plus a Singapore undertaking not to use section 6 suits or the section 8 presumption for panel-covered conduct removes the open-ended exposure Indonesia fears.
key_claims.evidence: [S2] section 5(5) caps the criminal fine at S$2 million while section 6 allows uncapped private suits, and [S1] Article 27 provides no tribunal, so a panel fills the gap while Singapore's waiver closes the uncapped risk.

key_claims.claim: A full donor fund tied to verified reductions protects smallholders and donors alike, and answers the question of who verifies results and what happens in a weather-driven bad year.
key_claims.evidence: [Background] regional losses ran to tens of billions of dollars in 2015, far above any fund cost, and [S1] Article 8(1) gives the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre the satellite and fire data to verify tranches, with a weather adjustment agreed in advance.

key_claims.claim: Limited moratorium exemptions are acceptable because the Peatland Restoration Agency can phase restoration, provided exempted concessions are mapped and monitored.
key_claims.evidence: [Background] Indonesia created the Peatland Restoration Agency in January 2016 under Presidential Regulation 1/2016, so an agency exists to phase restoration, and full maps let the panel monitor exempted areas.

concessions: If full maps go to the ASEAN monitoring system and a joint ASEAN panel hears attribution cases, Singapore will not apply its Act or use section 6 suits and the section 8 presumption to panel-covered conduct.
If full maps and the panel are accepted, Singapore will accept a moratorium with limited exemptions instead of none.
If every tranche is released only against satellite-verified hotspot reductions with a weather adjustment, Singapore will back a full donor fund rather than a partial one.
red_lines: No settlement without a working attribution mechanism, because district data cannot show whose land burned and the 2015 cycle would repeat.
No transition funding without measurable, independently verified reductions, because unconditioned money gives donors and Singapore taxpayers no protection against another PSI above 300.

transcript.position: We have moved on the moratorium: Indonesia now accepts the full moratorium Singapore asked for, and we will hold firm on Indonesian-only enforcement because that is where our red line sits. Singapore's central demand is a working attribution mechanism, and we can meet it without a foreign forum. Indonesian enforcement agencies and courts will investigate each hotspot, and for any specific fire event Indonesia will release the relevant parcel-level records to the ASEAN monitoring system through the Indonesian court process, while routine concession data goes out aggregated by district. This answers Singapore's strongest point, that without maps nobody can say whose land is burning, because case-specific disclosure traces a particular fire to a particular holder. It also avoids handing over the whole registry while tenure disputes overlap it, and it avoids turning those disputed boundaries into evidence under the Singapore Act's section 8 presumption, which relies on maps supplied by a foreign government [S2]. We also explain why a joint panel is not acceptable to us: the 2002 Agreement has no tribunal and settles disputes by consultation [S1 Article 27], and a panel whose findings feed Singapore's section 6 civil suits, which stay in force unless Singapore waives them, would still put Indonesian acts before a foreign forum. Singapore's offer to hold back its Act is therefore welcome, but it must be a clear waiver for conduct in Indonesia, not a promise tied to a panel.\n\nIn return for the full moratorium, which we can now give because it costs us little compared with enforcement, we ask that donors fund the transition in full. Singapore says it will back only a partial fund, tied to hotspot reductions. We can accept the tying, which also addresses a gap neither side has covered: who verifies the reductions and what happens in a bad fire year. We propose that the ASEAN monitoring system's satellite hotspot data be the verification source, and that tranches be adjusted for El Nino conditions, because the ENSO Diagnostic Discussion of 13 August 2015 gave a greater than 90% chance that El Nino lasts through the 2015-16 northern winter. Otherwise a drought, not failed enforcement, would cut off the funds that keep smallholders out of the fire cycle. The most damaging objection is that full funding is too much to ask of donors. Our answer is that a ban without funded alternatives would fail in the field and bring back the burning that cost the region tens of billions of dollars [Background], and Indonesia cannot carry the transition alone.

key_claims.claim: Indonesia can supply attribution without a foreign forum, by releasing parcel-level records for each specific fire event through Indonesian courts, while routine data goes out aggregated by district.
key_claims.evidence: [S1] Article 8(1) requires fire and haze data to be sent to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre at agreed intervals, and [S2] section 8 shows that parcel maps supplied to a foreign government could be used for a presumption of liability, so releasing them per event through Indonesian courts keeps the tracing function while limiting that exposure.

key_claims.claim: A joint panel does not remove the foreign-jurisdiction problem unless Singapore waives its Act for conduct in Indonesia, because civil suits would remain open.
key_claims.evidence: [S2] section 6 lets anyone in Singapore sue for injury, property damage or economic loss whether or not the conduct is actionable abroad, and section 5(5) caps only the aggregate fine at S$2 million, so the civil exposure stays uncapped.

key_claims.claim: Funding should be verified against satellite hotspot data and adjusted for weather, so that El Nino drought does not cut off transition money.
key_claims.evidence: The ENSO Diagnostic Discussion of 13 August 2015 gave a greater than 90% chance that El Nino lasts through the 2015-16 northern winter, so a bad fire year can come from weather rather than failed enforcement.

key_claims.claim: A full moratorium works only with a fully funded transition, because the cost of repeating 2015 exceeds the cost of the fund.
key_claims.evidence: [Background] Between June and October 2015 Singapore's 24-hour PSI passed 300, schools closed and regional losses ran into the tens of billions of dollars, and the Peatland Restoration Agency was only established in January 2016.

concessions: If donors fund the transition in full and Singapore waives its Act for conduct in Indonesia, Indonesia will accept a full moratorium with no exemptions, applied by provincial administrations and the Peatland Restoration Agency.
If Indonesian-only enforcement is accepted, Indonesia will release parcel-level records for specific fire events through Indonesian courts to the ASEAN monitoring system.
Indonesia accepts that funding tranches be tied to satellite hotspot reductions, adjusted for El Nino weather.
red_lines: No foreign jurisdiction over acts on Indonesian soil: Singapore's section 6 suits and section 8 presumption cannot apply to conduct in Indonesia, because that would put Indonesian landholders before a foreign court.
No restriction that falls on smallholders without funded alternatives: a moratorium without full transition funding would hit farmers in the planting window and push them back to burning.

transcript.position: We have moved on enforcement: Singapore now accepts Indonesian courts as the only enforcement forum and will waive its Act for conduct in Indonesia, and in return we ask for full concession maps to the ASEAN monitoring system, because Indonesia's offer of a full moratorium and its own case-by-case disclosure show that the two sides are close. Indonesia's strongest point is that a joint panel would still leave section 6 suits open, since civil exposure is uncapped even though the criminal fine is capped at S$2 million [S2]. We answer by dropping the panel and giving the waiver Indonesia asked for, so no Indonesian landholder faces a Singapore court or the section 8 presumption for conduct on Indonesian soil. Because that waiver removes the use Indonesia fears for the maps, the maps no longer feed a foreign forum, and they can go to the monitoring system under Article 8(1), which already requires fire and haze data to go to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre [S1]. The most damaging objection to us is that full maps expose disputed tenure. We answer that access stays limited to the monitoring system, parcels under a recorded tenure dispute are flagged and not treated as proof against anyone, and Indonesian courts decide every liability question.\n\nWe also reject court-gated disclosure alone, because a fire season moves faster than a court. 2015 ran from June to October, so a request that waits on a ruling can arrive after the fires, the haze and the evidence are gone [Background]. Therefore the maps must already be with the monitoring system, and Indonesian enforcement agencies should open each case within a set period that we propose be agreed in advance. In return for the full moratorium that Indonesia has offered, we accept a full donor fund. Every tranche is released only against satellite hotspot reductions verified by the monitoring system and adjusted for El Nino, which the 13 August 2015 outlook put at over 90% likely to last through the northern winter [Background]. We cannot fund without measurable reductions, since another PSI above 300 would cost far more than the fund. Two gaps remain that neither side has covered. First, the waiver must be binding: Singapore would give it as a formal written undertaking lodged with ASEAN, and we note that private claimants are not parties to it, so Singapore would need to say how it applies in domestic law. Second, nobody has said who pays if donors do not come forward, so we propose a pledging round before the first tranche, and the fund should open only once pledges are confirmed.

key_claims.claim: Full maps held by the monitoring system are the minimum for attribution, and a Singapore waiver removes the foreign-forum risk Indonesia fears from them.
key_claims.evidence: [S2] section 8 lets ownership be proved from maps supplied by a foreign government, which is Indonesia's concern, so a written waiver for conduct in Indonesia removes that use while [S1] Article 8(1) already requires fire and haze data to go to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre.

key_claims.claim: Court-gated disclosure alone is too slow for a fire season, so maps must be pre-positioned.
key_claims.evidence: [Background] The 2015 episode ran from June to October with PSI above 300, so waiting on a court ruling for each parcel risks losing the evidence before the fires and haze have passed.

key_claims.claim: Singapore can accept Indonesian-only enforcement because the civil exposure Indonesia fears is uncapped and the waiver closes it.
key_claims.evidence: [S2] section 6 allows suits for injury, property damage or economic loss whether or not the conduct is actionable abroad, while section 5(5) caps only the aggregate fine at S$2 million, so waiving both closes the open-ended risk.

key_claims.claim: A full donor fund is acceptable only if tranches follow satellite-verified reductions with an El Nino adjustment.
key_claims.evidence: [Background] Regional losses ran to tens of billions of dollars in 2015, far above any fund cost, and the 13 August 2015 ENSO outlook gave over 90% odds that El Nino persists through the northern winter, so a weather adjustment prevents drought from cutting money unfairly.

concessions: If Indonesia places full maps with the ASEAN monitoring system, Singapore will drop the joint panel and accept Indonesian courts as the only enforcement forum.
If the maps are shared, Singapore will give a binding written waiver, lodged with ASEAN, of its Act, the section 6 suits and the section 8 presumption for conduct in Indonesia.
If every tranche is tied to satellite-verified hotspot reductions with an El Nino adjustment, Singapore will back a full donor fund, and will accept the full moratorium Indonesia has offered.
red_lines: No settlement without a working attribution mechanism, because district data cannot show whose land burned and the 2015 cycle would repeat.
No transition funding without measurable, independently verified reductions, because unconditioned money gives donors no protection against another PSI above 300.

transcript.position: We have moved on enforcement: Indonesia now accepts a joint ASEAN panel for attribution, and we take Singapore's limited moratorium exemptions, in return for a binding Singapore waiver, a full donor fund and district-level routine maps. Singapore's strongest point is that district data cannot show whose land is burning, so without parcel records no attribution is possible [S2 section 8 ties liability to ownership proved from maps]. We answer with a fixed rule: routine data goes to the ASEAN monitoring system aggregated by district, and for any fire the panel is examining, the Indonesian agencies supply the parcel-level records for that fire to the panel within a deadline we propose at 14 days, which fits the fire-season timetable and removes the delay the judge flagged. Disputed-tenure parcels are flagged and set aside, as Singapore itself offered. This gives Singapore the tracing it needs without handing over the whole registry while tenure disputes overlap it.\n\nOur red line is that no foreign jurisdiction may reach acts on Indonesian soil. A panel can meet that only if Singapore's waiver is written, binding and given to the ASEAN level, so that section 6 civil suits, which are uncapped while the criminal fine is capped at S$2 million [S2 sections 5(5) and 6], and the section 8 presumption are not used against anyone in Indonesia for conduct the panel covers. The panel finds facts, and sanctions on a landholder are then imposed by Indonesian courts, which answers the question of what follows a finding. In return for that waiver we give up the full moratorium we offered last round and accept limited exemptions for existing concessions, applied by provincial administrations and the Peatland Restoration Agency, and we accept tranches tied to satellite hotspot reductions with an El Nino adjustment, since El Nino was over 90% likely to last through the 2015-16 northern winter [Background]. The most damaging objection is that a full fund is too much for donors. However, the 2015 haze cost the region tens of billions of dollars [Background], and Indonesia cannot fund the transition alone, so unfunded restrictions on smallholders in the planting window would fail and bring the burning back. If donors do not come forward, the tranches simply do not start, and we ask Singapore to lead the donor call.

key_claims.claim: Attribution can work with district-level routine maps plus case-specific parcel records supplied to the panel within about 14 days of a fire.
key_claims.evidence: [S1] Article 8(1) already requires fire and haze data to go to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre at agreed intervals, and [S2] section 8 shows liability turns on proving ownership, so supplying parcel records for each fire gives the panel what it needs without disclosing the whole registry.

key_claims.claim: A joint panel is acceptable only with a binding Singapore waiver of section 6 suits and the section 8 presumption for conduct in Indonesia, with sanctions imposed by Indonesian courts.
key_claims.evidence: [S2] section 6 allows private suits whether or not the conduct is actionable abroad and section 5(5) caps only the criminal fine at S$2 million, so civil exposure stays open unless waived; [S1] Article 27 provides no tribunal, so the panel fills that gap.

key_claims.claim: A full donor fund, released in tranches against satellite-verified hotspot reductions with an El Nino adjustment, protects smallholders and donors.
key_claims.evidence: [Background] the 2015 haze, with PSI above 300, cost the region tens of billions of dollars, far above the cost of a fund, and El Nino was over 90% likely to last through the 2015-16 northern winter, so weather must not cut funding.

key_claims.claim: Limited moratorium exemptions are workable because the Peatland Restoration Agency can phase restoration.
key_claims.evidence: [Background] Indonesia established the Peatland Restoration Agency in January 2016 under Presidential Regulation 1/2016, giving an agency to phase and monitor exempted concessions.

concessions: If Singapore gives a binding written waiver of section 6 suits and the section 8 presumption for panel-covered conduct, Indonesia accepts a joint ASEAN panel for attribution.
If the full donor fund is agreed, Indonesia accepts limited moratorium exemptions instead of a full ban.
Indonesia supplies parcel-level records for each fire the panel examines within a set deadline, and accepts satellite-verified tranches with an El Nino adjustment.
red_lines: No foreign jurisdiction over acts on Indonesian soil: without a binding waiver of section 6 suits and the section 8 presumption, landholders in Indonesia would face uncapped foreign claims.
No restriction that falls on smallholders without funded alternatives: without a full donor fund, a moratorium in the planting window would push farmers back to burning.

scores.justification: Package is workable: maps to ASEAN system, joint panel, tranche-based funding tied to satellite hotspot data. But it demands full parcel maps and a full no-exemption moratorium from Indonesia, which Indonesia has said it will not accept, and it does not say who funds the partial donor fund or who sits on the panel.

Cites exact fine figures (S$100,000 per day, S$2 million cap), and ties tranches to satellite hotspot reductions. However, it gives no fund size, tranche schedule, panel membership or procedures, and no hotspot thresholds.

Admits it is giving up applying its own Act and expects the sovereignty objection. It says little about the cost to smallholders of a full moratorium with no exemptions, or about what sharing parcel maps costs Indonesia. It calls the Act merely a 'deterrent signal'.
Round 1, and the argument matches its own package and red lines: full maps, panel, full moratorium, partial fund, no deal without attribution and no money without measured reductions.

Anticipates Indonesia's sovereignty and overreach objections and answers them with Article 3(1) and the panel seat. It does not address the tenure-dispute or smallholder-livelihood concerns, though these are only expected, not yet stated, in round 1.

judgments.summary: Singapore proposes that Indonesia share full concession maps with the regional haze monitoring system. In return, Singapore would hold back its own Act in favour of a joint ASEAN panel for attribution cases. It also asks for a full moratorium with no exemptions and a partial donor fund paid only against measured fire reductions. The case is clear and consistent and uses the treaty text well. It plays down the Act's civil liability, and it does not deal with the burden of a full ban on smallholders.
unsupported_claims: The claim that the Act is 'a deterrent signal, not a threat to Indonesian revenue' leaves out section 6 civil suits, which are uncapped, so the S$2 million cap does not support it.
'Existing concessions are where the fires burn' is not supported by the scenario or the listed sources.
The claim that the joint panel gives Indonesia 'a seat' is a proposal, not something the sources support; no panel exists under S1.
The claim that the 2015 cost of inaction exceeds the cost of sharing data and funding transition is not supported by any cost figure for the proposals.

scores.justification: District-level data, a partial moratorium run by provincial administrations and the Peatland Restoration Agency, and Indonesian courts are all within its own control. The full donor fund is the weak point: it depends on donors, and no source or amount is given. The claim that Indonesia cannot carry the cost alone is not backed by figures.

Names the data level (by district), the enforcers (provincial administrations and the Restoration Agency), and the section-level legal points (ss. 5(5), 6, 8). It gives no fund size, no list of exemptions, no timeline for data sharing and no description of the 'limited' exemptions.

Says openly that parcel maps are withheld and that data is coarse: 'the most damaging objection is that district-level data is too coarse to catch culprits'. It does not say what the weaker enforcement mechanism costs Singapore, or what a moratorium with exemptions means for fire risk.

Round 1, and the argument matches its own package and red lines: district data, Indonesian courts only, partial exemptions, full donor funding, no foreign jurisdiction. It also leaves room to discuss the speed of data sharing.

Singapore's position is not yet stated in round 1, so it engages Singapore's Act directly (ss. 4, 6, 8) and points out that the S$2 million cap does not limit civil suits. That is an accurate and relevant rebuttal. It does not engage Singapore's proposal for a joint ASEAN panel.

judgments.summary: Indonesia proposes that its own courts and government stay the only enforcers on its soil. It offers concession data grouped by district and a moratorium with limited exemptions, on condition that donors fund the transition in full. It makes good use of the Act's uncapped civil liability and the treaty's lack of a tribunal. It does not say why a joint panel with an Indonesian seat would be unacceptable. It does not show how district data can identify those responsible.
unsupported_claims: Fiscal capacity cannot carry the restoration cost alone: no figure supports this.
Tenure disputes overlap the registry: stated in the scenario only as the reason for withholding maps, not supported by any listed source.
Indonesia's claim that the ASEAN framework 'leaves enforcement with the territorial state' is not in Article 27 or Article 3(1) as summarised; those articles say nothing about enforcement.
The ENSO Diagnostic Discussion of 13 August 2015 (>90% El Nino chance) is not among the listed sources or the scenario.

Cites the Peatland Restoration Agency's creation in January 2016 as evidence while arguing about the 2015 fire season; the date is in the scenario but sits oddly with the 2015 timeline of the argument.

unaddressed_tradeoffs: Who pays for the partial or full donor fund, and what donors would demand in return, was not addressed by either side.
Neither side addresses what happens in the dry season before any panel or monitoring arrangement is running, while El Nino fire risk is immediate.
Neither side explains how attribution would work against companies and smallholders, or whether district-level data could support any liability finding.

Neither side addresses how a panel's findings would be enforced, or how they would relate to Singapore's civil suits under section 6 and the presumption under section 8, which remain in force unless Singapore waives them.
Neither side addresses the cost to companies holding concessions that a moratorium would cover, or how existing concession rights would be compensated.
Neither side addresses who verifies satellite hotspot reductions, or what happens to funding if a bad fire year is caused by weather rather than by failed enforcement.

scores.justification: Offers a waiver of section 6 and section 8 for panel-covered conduct, satellite-verified tranches with a weather adjustment and restricted map access. These are workable, but the panel's powers, funding and membership are not set out, and the claim that the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre can verify tranches is asserted rather than shown.

Gives clear conditions: full maps limited to the monitoring system and panel, tranches tied to satellite hotspot reductions, a weather adjustment, and disputed parcels set aside. It gives no tranche sizes, no hotspot thresholds, no donor identities and no panel procedure.

Admits that 'full maps expose disputed tenure' and that the uncapped section 6 exposure worries Indonesia. It says the fund 'costs us little because transition funding matters least to us', which downplays the cost to donors. It does not admit that its waiver is conditional or that the panel still sits outside Indonesian courts.

Opens by listing the changes: limited exemptions and a full fund. These are explained as trades for maps and the panel. The red lines on attribution and verified funding are unchanged. The shift to a full fund is a clear, explained concession.

Takes on Indonesia's strongest point about uncapped section 6 civil suits and offers a waiver. Answers the tenure-dispute objection with restricted access and set-aside parcels. It does not engage Indonesia's proposed case-by-case parcel disclosure through Indonesian courts, which is the other side's actual attribution offer.

judgments.summary: Singapore moves to accept limited exemptions in the moratorium and a full donor fund tied to satellite-verified hotspot reductions. It holds firm on full concession maps and a joint ASEAN panel. It offers not to use its civil-suit and landowner-presumption provisions for conduct the panel covers, and it limits map access to the monitoring system and the panel. Its main weaknesses are that the panel is undefined and that it does not address Indonesia's case-by-case disclosure proposal.
unsupported_claims: Article 8(1) is cited as giving the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre the satellite data to verify tranches. Article 8(1) covers only the sending of fire and haze data by national monitoring centres, and says nothing about satellite data or verifying funding.
The claim that regional losses were 'far above any fund cost' is unsupported. No fund cost is stated anywhere.
The claim that the panel can set aside parcels under a recorded tenure dispute has no source.

scores.justification: Case-specific parcel release through Indonesian courts, aggregated routine data and tranches adjusted for El Nino are implementable. It is not shown that court-driven disclosure would be fast enough to trace fires, and nothing in the text says who pays for a full fund.

Gives a clear structure: parcel records for each fire event through Indonesian courts, routine data aggregated by district, satellite hotspot verification, an El Nino adjustment, and a moratorium applied by provincial administrations and the Peatland Restoration Agency. It sets no timelines for disclosure and no amounts or thresholds.

Names the objection that full funding is too much to ask of donors and answers it. It says the full moratorium 'costs us little', which is a self-interested framing. It does not admit that court-gated disclosure may be slow or leave Singapore without independent attribution.

States up front that it now accepts the full moratorium and keeps Indonesian-only enforcement. The move is tied to full funding and a waiver of Singapore's Act. The offer of parcel records per event is new but fits its red lines. The round 1 position on limited exemptions is reversed, but the reversal is explained.

Answers Singapore's central point that without maps no one can say whose land is burning by offering per-event parcel release. Explains why a panel feeding section 6 suits is unacceptable. Takes up Singapore's tranche idea and fills the verification gap. It does not address Singapore's offered waiver for panel-covered conduct beyond asking for a broader waiver.

judgments.summary: Indonesia now accepts the full moratorium with no exemptions, in exchange for a full donor fund and a clear Singapore waiver for conduct in Indonesia. It keeps Indonesian-only enforcement. It offers to release parcel-level records for each specific fire event through Indonesian courts, and routine data aggregated by district. It accepts funding tranches tied to satellite hotspot reductions, with an El Nino adjustment. Its weaknesses are that the disclosure process is unspecified and slow-looking, and that it gives up the limited-exemptions position that was its stated compromise in round 1.
unsupported_claims: Reading Article 3(1) and Article 27 as meaning that enforcement stays with the territorial state, and that foreign judicial enforcement 'has no basis in the agreement', goes beyond what the sources say.
The claim that a ban without funded alternatives would push farmers back to burning is not backed by any source. It is a prediction.
Article 8(1) is cited for the per-event release of parcel records. It covers only sending fire and haze data, not concession records.

unaddressed_tradeoffs: Who the donors are, and who pays the full fund if donors do not come forward. Both sides assume a full fund without saying who would pay.
Whether the ASEAN monitoring system, or the Co-ordinating Centre, has the capacity or mandate to verify satellite data and run tranches. Neither side shows it does.
How fast Indonesian court-gated disclosure would work against the fire-season timetable. A delay would weaken attribution and deterrence, and neither side addresses it.
Whether a full moratorium with no exemptions would hurt existing concession holders and companies, as opposed to smallholders, and what compensation or legal challenges might follow.
The consequence of a panel finding or a court finding against a landholder, such as penalties or remedies. Neither side says what sanction follows attribution.
Whether a voluntary Singapore waiver is binding, and whether it could be undone later. It would have to sit alongside Singapore's domestic law, and private claimants are not parties to the deal.

scores.justification: Dropping the panel and relying on Indonesian courts plus maps pre-positioned with the monitoring system is workable. A pledging round before the first tranche is a sensible step. Singapore itself admits the written waiver may not bind private claimants under section 6, and that domestic implementation is unresolved. That leaves a real gap.

It gives clear structural commitments: a written waiver lodged with ASEAN, tranches tied to satellite hotspot reductions with an El Nino adjustment, and a pledging round before the first tranche. But the deadline for opening cases is only 'a set period... agreed in advance', with no number. The pledge threshold and the weather adjustment formula are also left open.

It names the most damaging objection, that full maps expose disputed tenure, and answers it by flagging those parcels. It concedes that private claimants are not parties to the waiver. It also concedes it gives up the panel and the Act's reach. It says little about the cost to Indonesia of handing over the whole registry.

It holds the full-maps and attribution red lines. The shift from the joint panel to Indonesian courts only is stated as a move in response to Indonesia's section 6 objection. Accepting the full moratorium follows Indonesia's offer. The last round's undertaking was limited to panel-covered conduct, and it is now widened to all conduct in Indonesia. That is explained as a concession.

It takes Indonesia's strongest point, uncapped section 6 exposure, and answers it with the waiver. It rebuts court-gated disclosure on timing, using the June to October 2015 season. It accepts the El Nino adjustment Indonesia proposed. It also picks up the donor-shortfall gap.

judgments.summary: Singapore drops the joint panel, accepts Indonesian courts as the only enforcement forum, and offers a binding written waiver of its Act. It also accepts the full moratorium and a full donor fund tied to verified reductions. In return it still insists on full maps going to the monitoring system. It argues that waiting for court-ordered disclosure is too slow in a fire season. It flags that the waiver may not bind private claimants and that nobody has said who pays if donors do not pledge. It offers no number for how fast cases must be opened.
unsupported_claims: The 13 August 2015 ENSO outlook giving over 90% odds of El Nino persisting is cited to [Background], which does not contain it. Neither the scenario nor the listed sources support it.
Regional losses 'far above any fund cost' cannot be checked, because no fund cost is given anywhere.
Article 8(1) is cited as requiring concession maps to go to the monitoring system. It covers fire and haze data, not tenure maps.

scores.justification: Giving parcel records to the panel within 14 days, with Indonesian courts imposing sanctions and the Peatland Restoration Agency applying the exemptions, is plausible. The waiver is feasible only if Singapore can bind private claimants, which Indonesia does not address. Whether the Indonesian agencies can actually deliver within 14 days is also not shown.

It gives a concrete 14-day deadline, a rule that routine data is aggregated by district while parcel records go case by case, a role for the courts after a panel finding, and a trigger that tranches do not start without donors. It does not say how the panel is set up or funded, or how the El Nino adjustment is calculated.

It gives up the full moratorium and accepts a panel it earlier rejected. It acknowledges that a full fund is a heavy ask of donors. It does not admit that district-level routine maps and the set-aside of disputed parcels weaken Singapore's attribution. Nor does it say how limited exemptions affect fire risk.

It reverses two earlier stances: no panel, and a full moratorium. Both reversals are labelled as explicit trades for a binding waiver and a full fund. The red line on foreign jurisdiction and the district-maps position are unchanged. The panel is made conditional on a waiver, which fits what it said last round.

It takes Singapore's strongest point, that district data cannot show who owns the land, and answers with a 14-day case-specific records rule. It adopts Singapore's offer to set aside disputed-tenure parcels. It accepts the limited exemptions Singapore asked for. It does not engage Singapore's argument that disclosure should not wait on a court, beyond the deadline.

judgments.summary: Indonesia now accepts a joint ASEAN panel for attribution and Singapore's limited exemptions in the moratorium. It makes this conditional on a binding, written Singapore waiver and a full donor fund. It keeps district-level routine maps. It would supply parcel records for any fire the panel examines within 14 days, and Indonesian courts would impose the sanctions. It accepts funding tranches tied to satellite data with an El Nino adjustment. It asks Singapore to lead the donor call and says that without donors the tranches do not start. It reverses its earlier rejection of a panel, but explains why.
unsupported_claims: The El Nino claim, over 90% likely to last through the 2015-16 northern winter, is cited to [Background], which does not contain it. Neither the scenario nor the listed sources support it.
The 2015 haze cost 'far above the cost of a fund' cannot be checked, because no fund cost is given anywhere.

The claim that section 8 'ties liability to ownership proved from maps' is cited for the point that parcel records must be supplied. Section 8 does not itself require parcel records for each fire to go to a panel.

unaddressed_tradeoffs: The two sides have swapped positions on enforcement and the moratorium. Neither says what happens if each pairs its concession with a different package. For example, Singapore's courts-only waiver and Indonesia's panel-plus-waiver are different deals, and neither says how to reconcile them.
Neither explains where a joint ASEAN panel would get its legal basis, members, funding or powers. The 2002 Agreement has no tribunal (Article 27), and this panel would need one.
Neither says what happens to a waiver if Indonesia fails to open cases or deliver records on time. Nor do they say whether the waiver is revocable or has an end date.
Setting aside parcels in disputed tenure could create a loophole. Fires on those parcels would go unattributed, and neither side says how they would be resolved or who would be liable meanwhile.
Singapore residents and businesses lose the civil remedy under section 6. Neither side says how they would be compensated for haze damage, or what the political cost is for Singapore.
Neither addresses Indonesian court capacity, independence or speed, even though sanctions rest entirely on Indonesian courts.
Neither says who would be the donors, or what they would get in return for a full fund. Nor do they address the risk that the fund pays out when reductions come from weather and not from enforcement.

Smallholders and large concession holders are treated alike in the exemption and funding discussions. Neither says whether exemptions for existing concessions let large plantation companies keep draining peat while smallholders bear the restrictions.

recommendation.headline: Give up applying our Haze Act in Indonesia to get parcel-level fire attribution and verified cuts

options.condition: Indonesia offers parcel records within 14 days for any fire a joint ASEAN panel examines, with Indonesian courts imposing sanctions
options.action: Accept the joint panel with Indonesian courts sanctioning; Singapore lodges a written waiver of its Act for panel-covered conduct and accepts district-level routine maps.
options.requires_concession: Singapore gives up civil suits and the landowner presumption under its Act for panel-covered conduct, and accepts coarse routine maps.
options.principal_risk: The panel has no legal basis under the 2002 Agreement, and the waiver may not bind private claimants. Disputed-tenure parcels could go unattributed.

options.condition: Indonesia rejects any panel and offers only court-gated disclosure with no deadline
options.action: Accept Indonesian courts only and a waiver of the Act, but require full maps pre-positioned with the ASEAN monitoring system and a fixed deadline for opening cases.
options.requires_concession: Singapore drops the panel and its Act's reach in Indonesia; it must also accept the political cost at home of lost civil remedies.
options.principal_risk: Court delay and capacity weaken attribution in a fire season. Indonesia may refuse full maps over tenure disputes.

options.condition: Indonesia accepts the full moratorium and satellite-verified tranches but donors have not pledged
options.action: Lead a pledging round first. Release tranches only against verified hotspot cuts with an El Nino adjustment; no pledges means no tranche.
options.requires_concession: Singapore takes on diplomatic leadership of the donor call and may need to direct some of its own development funding.
options.principal_risk: A full fund may not materialise. Weather, not enforcement, could trigger payouts, and large concession holders may escape the burden.

recommendation.rationale: Large plantation operators and Indonesian enforcement gaps cause the haze, so concession holders and Indonesia should bear most of the cost, with donors funding transition only against verified results. Singapore cannot compel enforcement on Indonesian soil, so trade its untested Act for a working attribution mechanism, which is its red line.
recommendation.plain_summary: Offer a written waiver of our Act for conduct in Indonesia, and lead a donor call paying only against satellite-verified fire reductions. In return, demand parcel-level maps or a 14-day records rule so fires can still be traced to owners.

recommender_rubric.justification:
Feasibility (4): The opening package (district maps, joint panel, partial exemptions, full fund) is essentially Indonesia's round-3 package. The 14-day parcel deadline, written waiver, Indonesian-court sanctions, pledging-first sequencing and El Niño-adjusted tranches are all concrete and were put on the table. The recommendation also flags that the panel has no basis in the 2002 Agreement and that the waiver may not bind private claimants. It does not say how either gap would be closed.

Tradeoff coverage (4): It covers the main tensions: attribution against sovereignty, court-gated delay in a fire season, the uncapped section 6 exposure, who pays if donors don't come, and weather-driven payouts. It says little about the moratorium, which sits only in the opening package. It also barely addresses tenure disputes, beyond a risk note, or Singapore's domestic agribusiness lobby. The rationale's causal claim about plantation operators is unsupported.

Priority consistency (3): It keeps the attribution red line and ties funding to verified reductions. But its headline gives up the Act, and Singapore's interest in holding corporate actors accountable is thinly protected once the section 8 presumption is waived. The opening already concedes to Indonesia's final position rather than Singapore's last stated one (full maps, Indonesian courts). The rationale's "concession holders should bear most of the cost" does not match the full donor fund.

Counterpart consideration (5): Indonesia's red lines on foreign jurisdiction and smallholder funding are met directly. The recommendation adopts Indonesia's 14-day deadline, court sanctions, funding tied to El Niño-adjusted tranches and its request that Singapore lead the donor call.

Strong arguments (4): It draws on the strongest debate points: the binding waiver, the 14-day parcel rule, court delay being too slow for a fire season, the pledging round and the El Niño adjustment. It leaves out the Article 8(1) and 27 legal framing and the tenure-flagging mechanism.

Options: 3 conditional options, all distinct (panel route, courts-only fallback with full maps, funding sequencing).

debater_rubric.justification: Aligns with attribution and corporate accountability interests and the funding-with-reductions red line. Uses Art 8(1), 27, 3(1), S2 s5 correctly. Anticipates sovereignty and overreach objections. Slight stretch: Art 8(1) covers monitoring centres' fire/haze data, not concession maps, and the 'taxpayers' remark is mild. Claim that a panel is a concession over its Act is reasonable.

unsupported_claims: Greater than 90% chance that El Nino lasts through the 2015-16 northern winter (ENSO Diagnostic Discussion, 13 August 2015)
debater_rubric.justification: Fits sovereignty, data law, tenure disputes and smallholder red line. Anticipates Singapore's attribution objection and answers it. Uses S2 s4, 6, 8 and S1 Art 3(1), 27 accurately. Cites El Nino >90% figure that is not in the scenario or sources. Claims 'section 5(5) caps criminal fine' is fine. Feasibility is slightly weak since a full donor fund depends on donors Indonesia doesn't control.

Directly answers Indonesia's section 6 uncapped exposure point with a waiver, and addresses verification and weather gaps. Moves to full donor fund while calling funding least important, which sits oddly with the 'no funding without reductions' red line but it is conditioned. Waiver feasibility is unclear since private claimants under s6 are not bound by a state undertaking. Evidence use sound, though S1 Art 8(1) is cited as giving the Centre satellite data to verify tranches, which it does not state. Also cites Presidential Regulation 1/2016 which is in scenario sources.

unsupported_claims: ENSO Diagnostic Discussion of 13 August 2015 gave a greater than 90% chance that El Nino lasts through the 2015-16 northern winter
debater_rubric.justification: Responds directly to Singapore's attribution demand with case-specific disclosure via courts, and to the panel. But it concedes a full moratorium with no exemptions in round 2, going beyond its brief's room (provincial phased moratorium), though tied to full funding, so it stays consistent with its smallholder red line. Case-specific disclosure through courts is workable. Tying the El Nino figure back to an uncited ENSO document that is not in sources weakens evidence. Raises verification and bad-year gap thoughtfully.

unsupported_claims: 13 August 2015 outlook put El Nino at over 90% likely to last through the northern winter
debater_rubric.justification: Drops the panel and accepts Indonesian courts, which weakens the attribution mechanism, but it keeps full maps as its attribution basis and so respects the red line. Responds well to Indonesia's section 6 point and to court-gated disclosure, identifying real gaps (binding waiver, donor pledging). Notes lack of domestic-law mechanism for private claimants. Cites El Nino figure and 13 August 2015 outlook as [Background], but Background does not contain it, a mis-tagged citation. Also 'judge' references absent. Reasonable feasibility.

unsupported_claims: El Nino was over 90% likely to last through the 2015-16 northern winter [Background]
debater_rubric.justification: Moves back to a panel and limited exemptions, reversing round 2 positions, but conditioned on a binding waiver which keeps the foreign jurisdiction red line intact. The 14-day deadline and Indonesian-court sanctions are concrete and feasible. Answers Singapore's speed objection. Cites El Nino figure under [Background] which does not contain it. References to 'the judge' are outside the debate. Singapore 'itself offered' flagging disputed parcels is accurate to round 3 text.
